articles.title: Samsung Galaxy Unpacked 2026 live — the Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, Z Flip 8 and Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 are all official
articles.text:
Samsung Galaxy Unpacked 2026 live — the Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, Z Flip 8 and Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 are all official
We're live from Samsung's big day for foldables and more
Samsung's second big phone launch of the year is now over — and as expected, at the July edition of Unpacked 2026 saw the launches of several new Fold and Flip phones, plus the full reveal of Samsung's new Intelligent Eyewear smart glasses.
Leading Samsung's new foldables range are the new Z Fold 8 Ultra, passport-style Z Fold 8, and the updated Z Flip 8. The highlight, at least among the crowd, was the Z Fold 8, which likely gives us a hint of what to expect from the rumored iPhone Ultra.
But the most intriguing new devices were the range Intelligent Eyewear smart glasses, which Samsung's made in collaboration with Google. These will come in a range of designs when they launch "this Fall", from classic square and round-style frames to cat-eye-style silhouettes, and we've already had an early look at them.
You can read everything that happened at Samsung Galaxy Unpacked's July 2026 edition below. Which device are you most excited about? Make sure you also vote in our poll below...
Read all of our Samsung Galaxy Unpacked 2026 coverage
- I’ve spent an hour with the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra — and I need to upgrade my Z Fold 7 ASAP
- I went hands-on with the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, and this passport-shaped oddity has revived my interest in foldable phones
- 'Finally, we've got silicon-carbon' — why SuperSaf is just as excited as we are for the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra's new battery
- 'If, because of that, we stop innovation, we don’t go anywhere': we got a first look at Samsung Intelligent Eyewear, the smart glasses entering a fraught market worried about privacy
- I've tested the Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8, and its new camera features make it an excellent vlogging camera alternative — so long as you don't mind the middling image quality
- Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 review: slimmer, lighter, better
That's a wrap
So that's it for Samsung's second Galaxy Unpacked event of the year. We've already been hands-on with all of the devices, including the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, Z Flip 8, Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 and the Samsung Intelligent Eyewear.
There weren't many surprises given the leaks were so generous, but we did all the official pricing — and the hikes aren't quite as bad as many feared. Samsung's Intelligent Eyewear (surely they're going to get a snappier nickname) also looks very interesting, if it can navigate the Great Smartglasses Backlash.
It's time for smart glasses
As expected, Samsung's 'one more thing' at Unpacked is its Intelligent Eyewear — and it does looks pretty impressive.
Samsung has partnered with Gentle Monster and Warby Parker in its attempt to take on the Ray-Ban Meta glasses, which is something we already knew. But we've just learned a bit more about their design and specs, including a new hinge design that has a power slider next to it.
Samsung is claiming nine hours of battery life from a single charge with 'mixed use' — which is seemingly around 90 minutes of notifications, 30 minutes of calls, 35 AI conversations, 12 message read alouds, 60 minutes of music playback, nine photo captures, and three one-minute videos.
It also says you'll be able to charge them more than seven times overs using their case. They'll apparently be lighter than most AI glasses (although their exact weight is still TBC) and will be powered by a Snapdragon AR1 chipset.
The Intelligent Eyewear (surely there's a snappier name) will launch in the Fall, so sometime between September and November. But a big question remains unanswered, how much will they cost?
Google talks Gemini
Google's Rick Osterloh has stepped in to tell us about the Gemini features that'll be available on Samsung's new foldables — and its new smart glasses too.
Gemini Notebook (the new name for NotebookLM) will apparently come preinstalled on the new foldables and buyers will get six months of Google AI Pro too (after which, you'll have to pay, of course).
Gemini Intelligence will also be coming to new smartglasses from Samsung, Gentle Monster and Warby Parker — and we're about to hear more about those...
The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 looks hardcore
The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is here — it looks pretty similar to its predecessor from a couple of years ago, but there are quite a few upgrades under the hood.
Its engine is the new Snapdragon Elite processor, which apparently offers 32% better performance than before. The Watch Ultra 2 is also the toughest Samsung watch so far, with IP69K and 10 ATM waterproof ratings.
There are some pretty hardcore diving features too, including Samsung's own diving algorithm and nitrogen absorption monitoring. Basically, Samsung is gunning for Garmin here.
The Watch Ultra 2 starts at $699 with the Galaxy Watch 9 starting at $379, with the Watch Ultra 2 launching from August 7.
Enter the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
It's time to move onto smartwatches. Samsung's just revealed the Galaxy Watch 9, and it's promising some handy new software features.
These include sleep apnea detection, which is also coming to the Galaxy Ring — and apparently makes it the only FDA-cleared, over-the-counter ring device with that feature.
The Galaxy Watch 9 will also have "proactive" features that constantly monitor things like heart rate and heart rate variability, and crunch all these together into a new heart health score.
Samsung says it's partnering with iFit for its subscription fitness content, too. But the more exciting smartwatch is coming next...
Spider-Man drops in
A Spider-Man interlude has just broken up the foldables news, as we get a teaser from his newest movie plus a chat from Ned, who's shown off a 'Spidey Tracker' alongside camera footage from the Z Fold 8 Ultra.
It's back to reality now though, as Samsung moves onto Samsung Care+ and the Galaxy Card, its new Apple Card rival that was announced this week.
Samsung's 'thinnest Flip yet'
This should be the final foldable from today's Unpacked — Samsung's Lee Dunham has just announced the Z Flip 8, and it sounds like a decent upgrade.
There's seemingly a much better Flex Display experience, with boosts to Now Brief (including the option of adding your own custom cards). And it's a bit slimmer and lighter at only 6.1mm thick when folded, and weighing in at 180g. You also get the same ProVisual engine as you get on Samsung's other Galaxy phones.
The downside is that pricing for the Z Flip 8 starts at $1,199 (with pre-orders starting today), which means it's a bit pricer than last year.
Telephoto out, 'FanCam' in
Sadly, there's no telephoto camera on the Z Fold 8, which is a shame — but Samsung's seemingly quite proud of its new 'FanCam' feature.
This new AI feature helps you quickly edit videos into your choice of aspect ratio, while keeping the star of your video in the center of the frame. Pretty neat, if perhaps not as useful as a telephoto — though that's probably revealing of Samsung's target market for the Z Fold 8.
Now onto the Z Fold 8
This is the one most of us have been waiting for — Samsung's revealed its new passport-style Fold 8, and it got more of a reaction from the crowd than the Ultra.
Samsung's explaining the benefits of that more square display, claiming it bring "a whole new dimension to mobile gaming", while in portrait the 3:4 ratio makes it a good fit for reading.
I definitely like the form factor (in theory), and it's likely a hint of what Apple's going to bring with the iPhone Ultra. It's also apparently the "world's lightest fold" ever...
Camera boosts for the Z Fold 8 Ultra
Samsung is now talking cameras on the Z Fold 8 Ultra, leaning heavily on its Nightography skills and talking up its much-improved 50MP ultrawide camera.
It also has a 200MP main camera with an f/1.7 lens and a 10MP telephoto that gives you up to 3x optical zoom, which are similar to its Fold 7 predecessor.
First up, the Z Fold 8 Ultra...
Samsung's starting its Z Fold 8 Ultra promo with Flex Titanium, the new hinge design it announced last week that promises to make the crease less visible.
Also, there's battery news — it has largest-ever battery in a Galaxy Z Fold phone (at 5000mAh), and for the first time uses silicon carbon tech that we've seen in its many Chinese rivals — hooray...
AI and privacy are the hot topics
Samsung's TM Roh is on the stage right now talking about the "the importance of AI infrastructure", as he says Galaxy AI will be coming to 800 million devices by the end of the year. Now we're moving onto its foldables, starting with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra...
The Samsung Glasses are coming
That's a surprise, Samsung has just teased that the Galaxy Glasses are coming at today's event. But first, it's going hard on security and privacy...
And we're off
TechRadar's Phones editor Axel Metz has some final pre-Unpacked thoughts as we go through Samsung's pre-amble.
"I’m curious to see whether Samsung positions the shorter, wider Galaxy Z Fold 8 as its hero product this year — i.e. the foldable it hopes and expects people to buy — or simply as a more affordable alternative to the premium Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra," he says.
"In making the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Samsung is acknowledging that the taller, narrower form factor of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra isn’t very ‘Gen Z’, and with Apple rumored to be releasing a similarly sized iPhone Ultra later this year, I — and probably Samsung — expect this new aspect ratio to become the foldable mainstream. Where does that leave the Ultra in years to come?" he says.
Get your popcorn ready
We're just a minute away from the start of Unpacked, and the expected arrival of its new foldables and smartwatches.
A final thought from TechRadar's Editor at Large, Lance Ulanoff, who's at the event right now. "What may be missing from this event is any kind of surprise. Samsung is very leaky, and most of the excitement tends to be muted by the time they tell us what we already knew or read about somewhere," he says.
"For Samsung, the goal is to generate Apple-level energy for its latest foldables and any other products they pull out of their back pocket. It's especially important to build that kind of momentum before Apple begins its product rollout juggernaut in September," he adds.
Five minutes to go...
It's now just five minutes till kick off, and TechRadar's Lance Ulanoff has shared some final thoughts on this year's second Unpacked.
"We pretty much all know the shape of things to come, but I'm super curious to see the reaction from the crowd here and online. Is different better or just different? Can more fold shapes expand the market? Or can only Apple do that?" he says.
We won't have to wait long to find out...
What about the Galaxy Ring 2?
What's TechRadar's Senior Fitness & Wearables Editor Matt Evans most excited about at today's Unpacked?
"I'm most looking forward to the wearables — the Watch 8 was outstanding last year, and I’m hoping for more of the same on that front. But the hotly-rumored Watch Ultra 2 is going to be the real star. Plus, who knows? We may event get a hint about a Ring 2…", he says.
Samsung has already confirmed it's working on the Galaxy Ring 2 — and while it isn't expected to get a full launch today, we could well get a teaser at the end of the event (just as Samsung did for the original Ring).
A subtle hint?
We're taking our seats at London's Galaxy Unpacked 2026 event and noticed a nice little touch from Samsung.
When you remove the perforated portion of our lanyards, it's remarkably close to the expected shape of the Z Fold 8 that we've seen in leaks.
Still, if you want an even clearer idea of what's coming, check out the leaked marketing materials that have just landed for the Fold 8 series. Or you could just wait 15 minutes to see the real thing...
These last-minute leaks are looking quite official
We're now less than 30 minutes away from Samsung Galaxy Unpacked 2026, and the leaks are looking ever more convincing, with what appears to be official marketing imagery having now leaked too, as you can see above.
This shows off all three expected foldables — the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8.
The purple Z Fold 8 Ultra looks quite appealing, but hopefully the pink background is a sign that we'll get some brighter colors too.
Samsung's first smart glasses sound like Ray-Ban Meta rivals
Samsung could be about to make smart glasses more mainstream, as its first pair is rumored to be included in today's announcements, and the Samsung Galaxy Glasses as we're calling them for now have been extensively leaked.
A detailed new leak on WinFuture tallies with what we've heard before, including that these apparently won't have a screen, and will instead rely on cameras and access to Gemini, which should be able to see what you can.
They sound a lot like the Ray-Ban Meta glasses, and like those they apparently use a Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 chipset, which is now three years old. Still, with supposedly 9 hours of battery life, Gemini access, and a big brand name behind them, they could be a hit.
The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 might live up to its name
We're also expecting various wearables today, and WinFuture has spilled the beans on the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 and Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 in a detailed leak.
The latter could have a slightly larger and much brighter display than its predecessor, coming in at 1.52 inches and 5,000 nits, and joined by a colossal — by smartwatch standards — 800mAh battery, along with a build that's designed with divers in mind.
This is sure to be expensive, but the standard Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 should be a cheaper option for anyone who doesn't need all the bells and whistles offered by the Ultra. Sadly though we're not expecting a new Classic model this year.
All the specs have already leaked
Samsung might not have too many surprises today if you've been following the leaks and rumors, as WinFuture.de recently leaked complete specs lists for the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Z Flip 8.
Highlights if this leak is accurate include a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset for the two Z Folds and — at least in Europe — an Exynos 2600 for the Galaxy Z Flip 8.
We'll also apparently get a higher-capacity and faster charging 5,000mAh / 45W battery in the Z Fold 8 Ultra, but the real highlight could be the base Z Fold 8, since this is widely expected to have a new shorter, wider form factor, which according to this leak will allow for a 7.6-inch foldable screen and a 5.5-inch cover display.
A self-healing crease?
Samsung's upcoming foldables might not just have smaller creases than their predecessors, they could also have self-healing ones if the latest leak (above) is to be believed.
It's unclear how this would work, but perhaps it would ensure the crease doesn't become more visible over time. It also reminds us of the self-healing finish on the LG G Flex series, which could automatically fill in minor scratches.
It will be interesting to see how Samsung's take on this works, but if this leak is accurate then it could be Samsung's secret weapon against the upcoming foldable iPhone Ultra.
Brace yourself for price hikes
Some slightly less positive news from today's Galaxy Unpacked 2026 event is likely to be price hikes for the Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8.
A recent report from Korea (via Phone Arena) suggested that both foldables could be about $130 pricier than their predecessors. In the grand scheme of RAMageddon, that wouldn't be too bad — and the Fold and Flip series have never been the most affordable phones anyway.
Samsung has also already increased the prices of the Z Fold and Flip 7 series over the past year, so hopefully that will soften today's potential price rises...
If you host an event in London...
The umbrellas are already out at the Galaxy Unpacked 2026 queue. We've had what feels like months without rain in London, but right on queue the dark clouds are forming.
It's now just over 90 minutes till kick-off time, so hopefully we'll be ushered inside soon...
Will Samsung finally solve foldable creases?
There's a good chance that we'll see another big step towards crease-free foldables today. We recently visited Samsung Display's secret labs where it talked to us, among many other things, about its new "Flex Titanium Technology".
This includes a special structure at the fold to give added flexibility and help reduce crease visibility. We've recently more leaks on that theme — and while the image above doesn't look like a particularly fair comparison in terms of lighting, I'm hoping this new feature lives up to the hyper when we see it in person later.
We've landed at Unpacked
We're very keen here at TechRadar, so we've already arrived at the Galaxy Unpacked event in London, and it's very... quiet.
That's understandable, as we're still two hours away from kick-off and many international attendees will be coming from hotels much closer to the start time.
A London-based Unpacked is a rarity — last year, Samsung did a mix of US-based and virtual events, while this year's earlier Unpacked in February was in San Francisco.
You have to go back to 2012 for the last time London hosted Samsung's main event, which saw the arrival of the Galaxy S III...
What are you most excited to see?
We've done a full rundown of everything we're expecting to see at Unpacked 2026, so that's worth a read as we get closer to kick-off (in just over two hours).
But the short version is that we're expecting three foldables (a Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra and Z Flip 8), plus two Galaxy Watches (the Watch Ultra 2 and Watch 9), and (potentially) also Samsung's first smart glasses.
Which one are you most excited about? Let us know in the poll below...
The Z Fold 8 is winning the hype battle
The Galazy Z Fold 8 is emerging as the potential star of today's Unpacked event — and the foldable has just appeared in a new teaser poster (above).
It's the Z Fold 8's wider, passport-style design, which will likely separate it from the taller Fold 8 Ultra, that makes it the one I'm most interested in from today's launches. Partly because it also probably gives us an early peak of the iPhone Ultra's likely form factor.
We're expecting to see a 5.5-inch cover display and 7.6-inch inner display, both with a 120Hz refresh rate. The teaser poster matches some of the leaked dummy units that we saw earlier this year (below).
Welcome to Galaxy Unpacked 2026 (the sequel)
Hello, and welcome to our liveblog for Samsung's second big phone launch of the year, Galaxy Unpacked 2026.
We'll be reporting live from the London event, which kicks off at 9am ET / 6am PT / 2pm BST / 11pm AEST. But first, it's time to take you through all of the last-minute rumors on what we're expecting to see — and we certainly haven't been short of leaks...

articles.title: Garmin lance son premier bracelet connecté, sans écran ni abonnement
articles.text:
Garmin fait officiellement son entrée dans le secteur des bracelets connectés avec un modèle baptisé Cirqa, dépourvu d’écran et vendu 200 euros. Cependant, contrairement aux bracelets de Whoop et au Fitbit Air de Google, le bracelet de Garmin n’intègre pas d’abonnement mensuel pour profiter de l’ensemble de ses fonctionnalités. Caractéristiques, suivi du sport et de la santé, date de lancement : voici tout ce qu’il faut savoir.
Un bracelet sans abonnement
Avant toute chose, il faut souligner que le bracelet de Garmin n’intègre pas d’abonnement. Si certains entraînements et certaines analyses sont réservés à la version Connect+, l’essentiel des fonctionnalités du bracelet est accessible gratuitement. Par conséquent, son prix fixé à 200 euros est à relativiser.
En effet, le bracelet Fitbit Air de Google est vendu deux fois moins cher, soit à 99 euros, mais il intègre un abonnement (9 euros par mois ou 99 euros par an) pour pouvoir accéder à différentes fonctions, comme les conseils IA personnalisés, une analyse approfondie du sommeil ou encore le score de prédisposition quotidienne. Sur le long terme, cette différence de prix est donc à mettre en perspective.
Le Cirqa : un bracelet sans écran destiné au suivi du sport et du sommeil
Le premier bracelet connecté de Garmin intègre un boîtier de 47 x 27 mm, ainsi qu’un module de 14,8 g. Il permet de mesurer différents paramètres de santé, comme la fréquence cardiaque, le taux d’oxygène dans le sang (SpO₂), le niveau de stress, la température cutanée ou encore le suivi du cycle menstruel. Ces différents paramètres peuvent aussi être utilisés pour déterminer la Body Battery, soit le score de forme délivré par les montres connectées de Garmin.
Bien entendu, on retrouve aussi un suivi du sommeil qui comprend notamment l’analyse des différentes phases, un score de sommeil, la détection des siestes ou encore la variabilité de la fréquence cardiaque. À noter également la présence de « Smart Alarms », des alarmes intelligentes capables de réveiller l’utilisateur au moment le plus opportun, en fonction de ses phases de sommeil.
Au niveau du sport, Garmin annonce plus de 80 profils sportifs pour son bracelet. Ce dernier peut détecter automatiquement certaines activités. De son côté, l’utilisateur peut lancer son activité favorite en appuyant sur l’unique bouton présent sur le bracelet. Au passage, précisons qu’il est possible de se doucher ou de nager avec le Cirqa, vu qu’il résiste jusqu’à 5 ATM. Enfin, notons que Garmin annonce 10 jours d’autonomie pour son tout premier bracelet.
Vu que le bracelet ne présente pas d’écran, les données doivent être consultées via l’application Connect, disponible sous Android et iOS. Notez également que le suivi GPS s’effectue seulement via un smartphone connecté. Le Cirqa sera commercialisé à partir de ce 24 juillet 2026 dans plusieurs coloris : noir, bleu marine, vert olive, rose ou encore lin. Par ailleurs, deux tailles sont proposées (S/M et L/XL), tandis qu’un brassard vendu séparément permet également de porter le dispositif autour du bras.
👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.

articles.title: He probado el Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8: ahora sé exactamente para quién es este nuevo formato de plegable
articles.text:
El Galaxy Z Fold8 fue uno de esos teléfonos que, sin necesidad de hacer demasiado ruido, consiguieron que quisiera seguir teniéndolo en la mano. Volví a él varias veces durante la toma de contacto, atraído por unas proporciones que cambian bastante la sensación habitual de un plegable tipo libro. Cerrado resulta compacto y ancho; abierto, despliega una superficie que invita a probar contenidos y aplicaciones de otra manera. Después de años viendo evolucionar esta categoría, no daba por hecho que un diseño diferente pudiera despertar tanta curiosidad. Este lo consiguió.
Conviene ordenar la nueva gama porque Samsung ha cambiado la lógica de los nombres. La silueta alta que hasta ahora asociábamos al Galaxy Z Fold continúa en el Fold8 Ultra, mientras que el modelo sin apellido es el recién llegado con proporciones de pasaporte. A su lado permanece el Flip8, la alternativa compacta de plegado vertical. Al tener los tres delante, me quedó claro que el catálogo no se entiende como una escalera en la que cada teléfono es mejor que el anterior, sino como tres propuestas pensadas para usos y públicos diferentes.
Antes de seguir, te recordamos que los miembros de Xataka Xtra pueden acceder a descuentos, ventajas y oportunidades exclusivas en la tienda online de Samsung, además de a sorteos exclusivos, un servidor privado de Discord y un creciente catálogo de descuentos y ventajas en servicios digitales. Puedes sumarte a la comunidad por solo 30 euros al año.
Ficha técnica del Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8
|  | SAMSUNG GALAXY Z FOLD8 | 
|---|---|
| Dimensiones y peso | Plegado: 81,9 x 123,9 x 9,7 mm Desplegado: 161,4 x 123,9 x 4,5 mm 201 gramos | 
| pantalla plegable | Dynamic AMOLED 2X de 7,6 pulgadas Resolución QXGA+ (2.448 x 1.848 píxeles) 403 píxeles por pulgada Tasa de refresco: 1-120 Hz Vision Booster | 
| pantalla principal | Dynamic AMOLED 2X de 5,5 pulgadas Resolución QXGA+ (1.248 x 1.972 píxeles) 428 píxeles por pulgada Tasa de refresco: 1-120 Hz Vision Booster Hasta 3.000 nits Pantalla de baja reflectancia | 
| procesador | Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 para Galaxy | 
| Memoria ram y almacenamiento | 12/256 GB 12/512 GB 16 GB/1 TB | 
| cámara frontal | Pantalla principal: 10 MP, f/2.2, FOV 85º Pantalla plegable: 10 MP, f/2.2, FOV 100º | 
| cámara principal | Angular de 50 MP, dual pixel AF, OIS, f/1.8, FOV 85º Gran angular de 50 MP, dual pixel AF, f/1.9, FOV 120º | 
| batería | Dual de 4.800 mAh (típica) Carga rápida de 45W Carga inalámbrica de 20W Carga inalámbrica inversa PowerShare | 
| conectividad | 5G NSA/SA LTE Wi-Fi 7 Bluetooth 6.0 NFC GPS | 
| sistema operativo | Android 17 One UI 9 | 
| otros | Resistencia IP48 Galaxy AI Knox Now Brief Now Nudge | 
| precio | Desde 1.999 euros | 
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8, 256 GB, Teléfono Móvil, Blanco
El plegable que faltaba en la familia Galaxy Z
Los plegables no siempre transmitieron la madurez que vemos hoy. En sus primeras generaciones, el asombro convivía con dudas razonables: cuánto resistiría la pantalla, cómo envejecería la bisagra o si aquel diseño tendría verdadero sentido más allá de la novedad. Con el paso de los años he visto cómo Samsung iba respondiendo a buena parte de esas preguntas mediante cambios en construcción, peso, grosor y experiencia de uso. El Galaxy Z Fold8 llega en un momento distinto: ya no necesita demostrar que un teléfono puede plegarse, sino qué valor puede aportar al hacerlo.
El salto más evidente, al menos en diseño, llegó con la generación anterior. Cuando probé los Galaxy Z Fold7 y Flip7, encontré dispositivos mucho más afinados en grosor, peso y sensación en la mano, como si Samsung hubiera conseguido ordenar por fin muchas de las piezas que llevaba años ajustando. Ya no eran teléfonos que llamaban la atención únicamente por plegarse, sino productos sólidos y coherentes dentro de la gama alta. Precisamente por eso, la pregunta para esta octava generación no era sencilla: qué hacer después de haber dado uno de los pasos más importantes.
Después de ese salto, Samsung podía seguir varios caminos. Podía rediseñar por completo toda la serie, pero el elegido ha sido otro: conservar aquello que ya funcionaba, perfeccionarlo y añadir una tercera propuesta. Tras tener los nuevos modelos en la mano, entiendo la decisión. Podríamos decir entonces que Galaxy Z Fold8 es la consecuencia natural de mucho de lo que Samsung ha aprendido a lo largo de las siete generaciones. El resultado es una gama más amplia, no necesariamente una ruptura con lo anterior.
La primera impresión al coger el Galaxy Z Fold8 es precisamente esa: no parece un dispositivo experimental, sino un producto que llega con una idea muy clara de lo que quiere ofrecer. Su cuerpo más bajo y ancho cambia su presencia respecto a los plegables tipo libro que conocíamos, pero mantiene una sensación de construcción sólida. En la mano se siente bien equilibrado, elegante y cuidado en los detalles. Sus 201 gramos también ayudan: según Samsung, es el Galaxy Z Fold más ligero que ha fabricado hasta ahora.
Una de las primeras diferencias la noté incluso antes de abrirlo. Cuando cogí el Galaxy Z Fold8 cerrado, sentí que la relación con la pantalla exterior era distinta a la que tenía asociada a otros plegables tipo libro. Se trata de un panel de 5,5 pulgadas con relación 10:16, y durante esos primeros minutos me encontré utilizándolo más de lo que esperaba, sin sentir que estaba esperando el momento de desplegar la pantalla principal. Consultar mensajes, navegar o responder rápidamente resultaba natural, aunque habrá que comprobar cómo evoluciona esa sensación con un uso diario prolongado.
El cambio más evidente llegó al desplegar la pantalla interior de 7,6 pulgadas. Su relación 4:3 explica buena parte de lo que Samsung persigue con este modelo: no se trata únicamente de tener más superficie delante, sino de cómo está distribuida. Durante la prueba, leer, ver contenido en horizontal o moverme por distintas aplicaciones resultó especialmente cómodo. La sensación se acercaba más a utilizar una pequeña superficie de trabajo que a limitarme a abrir un móvil para verlo más grande.
La lectura fue uno de los primeros usos en los que encontré una diferencia clara. Al colocar el teléfono en horizontal, consultar artículos, documentos o libros electrónicos se parecía más a hacerlo en una pequeña tableta que en un móvil convencional. Las líneas de texto disponen de más anchura y la información se reparte de una manera que facilita permanecer más tiempo con el dispositivo abierto.
Más allá de leer o consumir contenido, este planteamiento también demuestra sus ventajas en la multitarea. Al utilizar el Galaxy Z Fold8 con varias aplicaciones abiertas, pude distribuir mejor la información y mantener más elementos a la vista al mismo tiempo. Es una forma de uso que cuesta explicar mirando únicamente una ficha técnica, porque aparece cuando empiezas a combinar tareas: consultar algo mientras escribes, comparar información o pasar de una aplicación a otra sin perder tanto contexto.
Los colores también forman parte del cambio de enfoque que percibí. Al tenerlo delante, la sensación no era la de un dispositivo pensado únicamente para un entorno profesional, algo que durante años ha acompañado a la imagen de algunos plegables tipo libro. El grafito ofrece una apariencia más discreta, mientras que el lavanda y especialmente el pistacho refuerzan una identidad menos corporativa. El formato pasaporte del Galaxy Z Fold8 aporta aire fresco a la gama y abre una nueva forma de entrar en el mundo de los plegables.
Después de tener ambos en la mano, me parece importante no entender el Galaxy Z Fold8 como una simple versión inferior del Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra. Los dos comparten el Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy, pero persiguen prioridades diferentes. El Ultra conserva la filosofía del Fold tradicional y suma una pantalla principal de 8 pulgadas y una cámara triple encabezada por un sensor de 200 MP, con un enfoque más marcado hacia la productividad y la creación de contenido. El Fold8 busca otra cosa: cambiar la interacción con el dispositivo desde las propias proporciones.
Ahora tengo bastante claro para quién es el Galaxy Z Fold8: para quien quiere un plegable tipo libro, pero no termina de encajar con las proporciones altas del Fold tradicional ni necesita el enfoque más ambicioso del Ultra. Es un dispositivo pensado para quienes valoran poder utilizar con naturalidad la pantalla exterior y, al abrirlo, disponer de un panel especialmente cómodo para leer, consumir contenido o trabajar con varias aplicaciones. El Flip8 sigue priorizando la compacidad y el Fold8 Ultra la productividad y la creación. Este Fold8 ocupa el espacio que quedaba entre ambos.
La decisión de añadir una nueva propuesta también se entiende mejor si miramos el camino que Samsung ha recorrido en España. En una conversación que mantuvimos a principios de julio con David Alonso, vicepresidente y responsable de Mobile Experience de Samsung Electronics Iberia, el directivo nos explicó que "el 93% de todos los plegables que se han vendido en España son Samsung". Es una posición de partida relevante, aunque no garantiza cómo responderá el mercado al recién llegado.
Como podemos ver, Samsung mantiene los otros dos diseños y añade una alternativa para quienes buscaban otra manera de utilizar este tipo de dispositivo. Quedan pendientes las pruebas más a fondo que veremos en la review del dispositivo. El Galaxy Z Fold8 ya se puede reservar en España desde 1.999 euros. Después de haberlo tenido en la mano, la conclusión de esta primera toma de contacto es sencilla: no estamos ante una ruptura con el pasado, sino ante una nueva dirección dentro de una familia que ya tiene mucho recorrido.

articles.title: Kimi K3 rocks the AI industry as Moonshot AI undercuts closed-source American competitors on price — but the huge 2.8T open-weight model still needs serious hardware to deploy at scale
articles.text:
Kimi K3 rocks the AI industry as Moonshot AI undercuts closed-source American competitors on price — but the huge 2.8T open-weight model still needs serious hardware to deploy at scale
Memory makers are the big winners, regardless of how it works out.
A new AI model from Chinese firm Moonshot AI has had its "DeepSeek moment," causing major disruption in the global AI market and spooking Western developers. Kimi K3 is an open-weight model, with 2.8 trillion parameters, making it the largest open-weight AI model ever released. Internal benchmarks have it competing with models like GPT 5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8, and Arena.ai awarded it the number one spot in its Frontend Code Arena test, even beating out Claude Fable 5.
It doesn't win every benchmark, and reports that suggest Kimi K3 is much slower than frontier models from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. All benchmarked results are drawn from API access, too, so can't be verified until Moonshot releases the weights on July 27.
But that hasn't reduced the impact of this model's release on the AI industry. With Kimi K3 cutting costs compared to the competition, it's drawing a lot of interest from companies hoping to reduce AI spend. For comparison's sake, OpenRouter tables Kimi K3 at $3/15 per million inputs and outputs. OpenAI's GPT 5.6 Sol is more expensive than that, at $5/30, and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 is $10/50. So, it's fair to say that Kimi K3 is incredibly competitive on price, especially when tabled against the costs of those closed-source Western AI models.
Microsoft is also considering Kimi K3 for Copilot, while the White House may ban Chinese models entirely. Meanwhile, memory makers are rubbing their hands together with glee, as Kimi K3 occupies up to 1.4 TB of memory, given its huge number of parameters.
Fast, cheap, or American?
The past few months have been full of talk about the frontier AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI. Mythos was big and scary until OpenAI had something equivalent. Then Fable debuted, and it was even better but not so scary anymore. Apparently.
But these models were also proving very expensive to run, at a time when companies with big AI deployments were questioning the return on that investment. Uber limited AI use by developers, and others killed the AI-boosting leaderboards they'd championed towards the end of 2025.
So when Moonshot debuted Kimi K3 with running costs a third that of western frontier models for the same results, the world took notice. In much the same way as DeepSeek's R1 debut in 2025 showcased how models could be trained for less -- even if there may have been some corporate espionage involved -- and Kimi K3 is holding up a similar mirror to Western frontier developers.
Where DeepSeek R1 was lean, though, Kimi K3 is huge -- so large, the developers are calling it the first open 3T-class system, and China's largest AI model to date. According to Bloomberg's sources, its sparsity ratio is the highest yet seen by any AI model. That's the measurement of how many parameters are activated for each task relative to the model's size, showcasing both Kimi K3's overall size and its impressive efficiency in the same breath.
This doesn't eclipse the most capable models from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI in every test. Arena.ai's rankings put it within the top 10 on most of its tests, but only coming out on top in a couple. But if Kimi K3 can offer results comparable to more expensive alternatives like Claude and ChatGPT, it's likely to draw a lot of interest from Western companies, and it appears to be already doing so.
Enough that it's revived calls for the U.S. to gatekeep access to international AI models, in a similar manner to how it recently pushed for companies to share exclusive model access with the U.S. government before a wider release.
In comparison, Moonshot is opening up Kimi K3 to the wider world. As part of releasing the model weights to the public, it will allow companies and organizations to run the model themselves without using Moonshot's cloud services, making adoption easier and potentially cheaper.
But it won't be cheap, as Kimi K3 still needs serious hardware investment to get up and running, by virtue of its massive VRAM requirements alone.
A Win for (Chinese) Memory Makers
As large companies with major AI deployments began to scale back their AI initiatives in 2026, there's been a growing concern that all that infrastructure everyone's been spending hundreds of billions of dollars on might not be needed. Meta just started selling excess compute in a pivot to cloud services, and xAI unloaded the entire compute capacity of Colossus 1 to Anthropic at a discounted rate.
But if Kimi K3 is the way the industry might go, hardware demands are unlikely to fall, and as Jevon's paradox suggests, greater efficiency is only likely to increase usage, not shrink it.
Those trillions of parameters need to be stored in memory, and Bloomberg's estimates suggest Kimi K3 will require close to 1.5 TB of memory. It would need masses of high-end Nvidia GPUs to deploy it effectively, making the number of companies and organizations that could actually run Kimi K3 at scale rather small.
So even those who do look to leverage Kimi K3 to reduce operating costs will still need powerful hardware, and specifically a lot of memory. This suggests that the major competition for cutting-edge models is not going to crater costs like we initially saw with DeepSeek R1 last year, which means memory makers are going to continue making money hand over fist, due to their outsized demand and limited supply.
But Chinese memory suppliers like CXMT are on the rise, and on track to eclipse Micron's DRAM wafer capacity by the end of the year. Smaller local AI models will also continue to be further optimized for domestic hardware, reducing the stranglehold that some large tech companies have on the AI supply chain.
Competitive, efficient, but unwieldy
Kimi K3 is an industry disruptor and is already raising questions over AI costs, capabilities, and access. It's shown that you don't need proprietary models locked to a specific service to achieve frontier-model capabilities. It's also cheaper to run, but Moonshot achieved this with a sparse model that still requires massive hardware investment to operate.
Even though Kimi K3 activates only a fraction of its trillions of parameters for each query, it still needs all of them to be stored. Deploying this model at scale requires substantial memory capacity, bandwidth, and interconnects, even if its compute demands aren't as strenuous.
The open-weight nature means it has very real potential to supplant usage away from Western frontier models in the short term, but it isn't about to change the story we've been told on required infrastructure. Kimi K3 needs the same kind of hardware to run as GPT 5.6 and Fable — which is likely to be far more of a limiting factor on its adoption than any kind of government blocks.
Jon Martindale is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. For the past 20 years, he's been writing about PC components, emerging technologies, and the latest software advances. His deep and broad journalistic experience gives him unique insights into the most exciting technology trends of today and tomorrow.

articles.title: US Treasury Secretary Bessent threatens sanctions against Chinese AI model makers - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
US Treasury Secretary Bessent threatens sanctions against Chinese AI model makers
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said today that the White House is going to examine some of the highest profile “open-weight” models from China to see if their creators have stolen the intellectual property of America’s top artificial intelligence frontier labs.
If evidence suggests that’s the case, the U.S. could respond with sanctions against the Chinese firms found guilty, he said.
In an interview with Fox Business, Bessent (pictured) said the Trump administration supports open-source models, but is dead against IP theft. “If we see, especially, that overseas models are stealing from our great companies, we have the ability to sanction them because of this theft,” he said.
Bessent’s comments come just days after one of China’s hottest AI startups, Moonshot AI, unveiled a new open-weights model called Kimi K3 that matches the performance of OpenAI Group PBC’s and Anthropic PBC’s most advanced models on some metrics. Chinese models are becoming increasingly popular with U.S. businesses, because they’re seen as more than good enough in terms of their capabilities, and cost far less money thanks to their open-source nature. It’s a trend that threatens to derail the business models of America’s top AI labs and prevent them from raising further capital.
On Monday, a report in Axios claimed that the Trump administration was even considering implementing a wholesale ban on open-source models from China, though officials have since distanced themselves from that report. Both Anthropic and OpenAI have publicly voiced concerns in recent months that foreign competitors are harvesting massive amounts of data from their models in order to use it to build their own, redeployed as open source technology. In April, the White House vowed to work with them to try and combat this perceived theft.
If the U.S. does implement sanctions against Chinese model makers, it would be a significant escalation of an increasingly bitter race to maintain leadership in the AI industry. The U.S. has already taken substantial steps to rein in China’s capabilities, restricting its access to the most advanced AI processors. But the sanctions would mark the first time it has targeted Chinese model makers directly.
China’s leading AI firms are accused of using a technique known as “model distillation,” which makes it possible to assimilate the capabilities of much larger models into smaller systems that are easier to run. The technique has been used by many American companies to create more efficient versions of their own models, and not everyone agrees it constitutes theft.
One of the biggest critics of critics of China’s AI labs is Microsoft Chief Executive Satya Nadella, who insinuated that it’s hypocritical of American firms to make such accusations. “While the great innovation that comes from model providers having fair use rights to train models on public data is needed, I find it ironic that the status quo is to then turn around and impose restrictive terms on distillation,” he wrote in an article on X last month.
— Satya Nadella (@satyanadella) July 12, 2026
It’s hard not to see Anthropic just as guilty as the Chinese firms it’s accusing, and U.S. law appears to agree that’s the case. Earlier this week, the Claude chatbot creator revealed it would start writing checks to authors as part of a $1.5 billion settlement it had agreed after a judge ruled that it had illegally downloaded and stored millions of copyrighted books that were used to train its models. Meanwhile, OpenAI is still embroiled in its own, long-running feud, having been sued by the The New York Times in 2023 for allegedly training its models on its content without permission.
Any sanctions imposed by the U.S. on Chinese AI firms may well be moot, however, if Beijing decides to make good on a recent threat of its own. Earlier this month, Reuters reported that Chinese officials are considering restricting the ability of foreigners to access its most advanced models, in response to similar moves made by the White House.

articles.title: Light Flip é um celular dobrável que leva o minimalismo a sério • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Light Flip é um celular dobrável que leva o minimalismo a sério
Lembrando vagamente o clássico Razr V3, Light Flip é um celular que traz apenas recursos essenciais para quem quer prevenir distrações.
Lembrando vagamente o clássico Razr V3, Light Flip é um celular que traz apenas recursos essenciais para quem quer prevenir distrações.
A Light ataca novamente. Falo de uma marca que é focada em celulares minimalistas. O recém-anunciado Light Flip segue essa proposta, tendo como diferencial o fato de ser dobrável, como o próprio nome indica. Só não espere encontrar uma tela externa no modelo — aqui, o conceito de minimalismo é levado a sério.
É impossível não lembrar do clássico Razr V3 ao olhar para o Light Flip, a não ser que você nunca tenha tido contato com o modelo da Motorola. Seja como for, eles só são semelhantes entre si no formato. O design e os recursos oferecidos pelo Light Flip são mais atuais, obviamente.
Para começar, o Light Flip exibe uma tela OLED fosca de 2,8 polegadas quando aberto. A parte inferior do aparelho traz um teclado numérico físico, bem como botões de navegação.
A parte traseira inferior do dobrável abriga uma única câmera com sensor de 50 megapixels. Já a área superior, que poderia dar acesso a uma tela, conta apenas com um curioso LED de notificações com formato de estrela (ou asterisco).
No comando da novidade está o chip octa-core MediaTek MT8873, que trabalha em conjunto com 6 GB de RAM e 128 GB de armazenamento interno.
É uma configuração de hardware não muito avançada, mas que promete dar conta do sistema operacional LightOS e de seus principais atributos, como navegador, reprodutor de áudio, discador, agenda e mapas.
Neste ponto, chegamos à verdadeira proposta do Light Flip: ser um celular que oferece apenas recursos essenciais para evitar que você se distraia com redes sociais, jogos e afins.
O aparelho contará com um SDK (kit de desenvolvimento de software) para permitir a criação de aplicativos por terceiros, mas não será nada tão amplo quanto o ecossistema do Android, por exemplo.
Se celulares minimalistas fazem sentido? Parece que sim, afinal, a Light existe desde 2014 e anunciou o seu primeiro celular, o Light Phone, em 2017. De lá para cá, outros modelos “antidistrações” foram lançados pela marca, com o Light Flip sendo apenas o anúncio mais recente.
Quem se animou com o Light Flip precisa saber que a novidade já pode ser reservada no site oficial, mas que os envios só começarão em abril de 2027.
O preço oficial é de US$ 299 (R$ 1.522 na conversão direta). Nos Estados Unidos, os compradores também poderão contratar um plano de telefonia com franquia de dados de 1 GB ao preço de US$ 39 por mês ou optar pelo plano de US$ 69 mensais que não tem limite de tráfego.
Não sei se eu compraria um. Mas admito que eu estaria disposto a testar o Light Flip por alguns dias para saber ele proporciona mesmo um efeito de “detox digital”.

articles.title: France just voted to ban kids under 15 from social media, but Australia's ban shows how hard that is to enforce
articles.text:
Overview: As social media algorithms come under increasing scrutiny, policies to ban children from services such as Facebook, X, YouTube, and Snapchat are gaining popularity across the globe. France has just become the latest country to pass such legislation – but data suggests the impact of Australia's earlier ban has been limited.
France's Parliament gave final approval on Tuesday to a law banning children under age 15 from social media, with the National Assembly voting 279 to 81 after the Senate had approved the text earlier the same day. The vote followed the Assembly's initial approval of the bill in January by a margin of 130 to 21.
President Emmanuel Macron, who strongly championed the legislation, wants it in effect before the new school year begins in September. The bill also bans smartphone use in high schools but exempts online encyclopedias such as Wikipedia, educational and scientific directories, and open-source software platforms such as GitHub.
The bill enjoyed unusually broad bipartisan support in France's traditionally divided parliament. Macron fast-tracked the legislation, hailing its passage as a "major step forward" and positioning France as the first country in the European Union to approve a blanket social media ban for minors.
Macron cited data from France's national public health agency indicating that one in two teenagers in the country spends between two and five hours each day using smartphones. Approximately 90% access the internet via phones daily, and more than half access social media on them.
The president has said the country aims to protect children's brains from being "manipulated," in his words, "neither by American platforms, nor by Chinese algorithms." Lawmaker Laure Miller, who authored the bill, said the legislation firmly establishes that social media is not harmless, arguing it causes children to read less, sleep less, and compare themselves to others more.
With the law now passed, France leapfrogs proposals still moving through other European countries, including Greece, Norway, Spain, and the UK. Greece aims to enforce a ban starting next year, and restrictions for under-16s are set to be introduced into the Norwegian and British parliaments by the end of 2026.
Australia became the first country in the world to attempt such a ban, in December 2025, but recent studies cast doubt on its effectiveness. Australia's eSafety Commissioner found that roughly seven in ten children who held social media accounts before the ban took effect still retained them three months later, and a study published in the British Medical Journal put the figure as high as 85%.
Regulators say Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, and YouTube have largely failed to enforce the removal of underage accounts. Most teenagers who kept access report never encountering an age-verification check, even though some circumvented restrictions using VPNs or other workarounds. France is also considering restricting VPN use to close a similar loophole.
In response to the noncompliance, the Australian government doubled the maximum penalty for infringing companies to $99 million AUD (about US$68 million). Australia's internet regulator, eSafety, is currently investigating Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, and YouTube for non-compliance.

articles.title: ¿Falso o real? Cómo identificar el nuevo fraude del CAPTCHA y qué hacer si caes en la trampa
articles.text:
La seguridad digital enfrenta una nueva amenaza que aprovecha la confianza de los usuarios en una de las herramientas más conocidas de internet: el CAPTCHA. Originalmente diseñado para distinguir humanos de bots mediante tareas simples como identificar imágenes o ingresar texto, el CAPTCHA se ha convertido en el último disfraz de una campaña de phishing que puede poner en riesgo tus datos y tu dispositivo.
La relevancia de este nuevo fraude radica en su capacidad para engañar a usuarios experimentados y en la velocidad con la que puede comprometer información confidencial. Detectar el engaño y saber cómo actuar es fundamental en un entorno donde las estafas digitales evolucionan constantemente.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo funciona el fraude del CAPTCHA falso
El ataque comienza cuando el usuario recibe una solicitud de CAPTCHA inesperada al navegar por un sitio web. A simple vista, la pantalla se parece a cualquier verificación legítima: cuadros de texto, imágenes para seleccionar o instrucciones para demostrar que no eres un robot. Sin embargo, la diferencia clave está en el tipo de tarea que solicita.
En lugar de pedir que resuelvas un puzzle visual o ingreses un código, el falso CAPTCHA te indica que ejecutes una serie de comandos en tu dispositivo, como “Windows + R”, seguido de “Ctrl + V” y “Enter”. Esta secuencia, lejos de ser una verificación de seguridad, está diseñada para que pegues y ejecutes un programa malicioso oculto, dando acceso a los estafadores a tus datos personales y cuentas sensibles.
PUBLICIDAD
¿Por qué es tan efectivo este fraude?
El éxito de esta estafa radica en la familiaridad. Los usuarios están acostumbrados a ver CAPTCHAs a diario y asumen que forman parte de la navegación segura. Al imitar el diseño y el lenguaje de los CAPTCHA reales, los estafadores logran que muchas personas sigan las instrucciones sin sospechar.
Además, el mensaje suele estar acompañado por frases como “verificación de seguridad” o “confirme que es humano”, lo que refuerza la sensación de legitimidad. Al ejecutar los comandos, el usuario puede instalar sin saberlo malware capaz de robar credenciales de email, banca móvil o cualquier otro dato almacenado en el dispositivo.
PUBLICIDAD
Claves para identificar un CAPTCHA falso
- Desconfía de solicitudes que pidan ejecutar comandos: Un CAPTCHA real nunca te pedirá que uses combinaciones de teclas del sistema ni que pegues líneas de código.
- Evita descargar archivos inesperados: Si tras la verificación se descarga automáticamente un archivo, no lo abras ni lo ejecutes.
- Verifica la dirección web: Los CAPTCHAs auténticos suelen estar asociados a sitios oficiales o servicios reconocidos.
- Presta atención a los detalles gráficos: Errores de ortografía, logotipos alterados o estilos visuales poco pulidos son señales de alerta.
¿Qué hacer si ejecutaste un CAPTCHA falso?
Si notas que tras interactuar con un CAPTCHA algo se descarga en tu dispositivo o seguiste instrucciones para ejecutar comandos, es crucial actuar de inmediato:
- Desconéctate de internet: Esto limita el acceso remoto de los atacantes a tus cuentas y dispositivos.
- Ejecuta un análisis de seguridad: Utiliza un software antivirus confiable para detectar y eliminar cualquier programa malicioso.
- Actualiza tu sistema y aplicaciones: Mantener el software al día ayuda a bloquear vulnerabilidades que los atacantes podrían explotar.
- Cambia todas tus contraseñas: Hazlo desde otro dispositivo seguro, especialmente para cuentas de correo, banca y tiendas online.
- Activa la autenticación de dos factores (2FA): Esto añade una capa adicional de protección en caso de que tus credenciales hayan sido comprometidas.
El fraude del CAPTCHA falso es un ejemplo más de cómo los ciberdelincuentes explotan rutinas digitales cotidianas para obtener acceso a información sensible. A medida que los usuarios se familiarizan con ciertas interfaces, los atacantes adaptan sus métodos para aprovechar esa confianza.
PUBLICIDAD
La mejor defensa es la prevención: evita ejecutar instrucciones que no entiendas, mantente informado sobre las nuevas tácticas de phishing y utiliza herramientas de seguridad actualizadas. Si tienes dudas sobre una solicitud de verificación, cierra la página y accede solo a sitios oficiales o de confianza.
Detectar y frenar a tiempo estos engaños es clave para mantener tu información segura en un entorno digital cada vez más desafiante.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Deezer : plus de la moitié des titres soumis chaque jour sont générés par IA
articles.text:
Deezer indique que les morceaux générés par intelligence artificielle dépassent pour la première fois la moitié des chargements quotidiens sur sa plateforme. En parallèle, la société annonce de nouvelles mesures de suppression visant les titres liés à la fraude ou non écoutés depuis plusieurs mois.
En avril 2026, nous rapportions que 75 000 titres générés par IA étaient envoyés chaque jour sur Deezer, soit 44% des dépôts quotidiens. Deux mois plus tard, ce volume a atteint 90 000 titres par jour en moyenne sur le mois de juin, une proportion qui dépasse donc désormais 50% du total.
90 000 morceaux générés par IA, chaque jour
Depuis le déploiement de son outil de détection en janvier 2025, Deezer observe une progression continue des morceaux générés par IA : 10 000 titres par jour au démarrage, puis 30 000 en septembre 2025, 50 000 en novembre, 60 000 en janvier 2026 et 75 000 en avril. Le cap des 90 000 titres quotidiens franchi en juin marque une accélération par rapport aux mois précédents, sur la base d'une moyenne mensuelle calculée par la plateforme.
L'entreprise précise que cette masse de contenus ne se traduit pas au niveau des streams. Il n'y a pas d'écoute massive de morceaux entièrement générés par IA. Ces derniers ne représentent que 1 à 3% des flux d'écoute sur Deezer. Il faut dire que depuis l'année dernière, Deezer les exclut systématiquement des recommandations et des playlists éditoriales. Deezer précise en revanche que jusqu'à 85% des écoutes générées par ces titres synthétiques provenaient de fraude en 2025, contre 8% pour l'ensemble du catalogue. Concrètement, ces écoutes frauduleuses visent à capter une part des sommes destinées aux ayants droit. Deezer indique les retirer du calcul des redevances, ce qui limite leur effet sur la rémunération des artistes.
Pour aller plus loin, la plateforme annonce la suppression prochaine des titres IA identifiés comme frauduleux, ainsi que de ceux qui n'ont pas été écoutés depuis au moins six mois. Cette seconde catégorie concerne les morceaux qui n'ont trouvé aucune audience depuis leur mise en ligne.
Deezer n'est bien évidemment pas la seule entreprise affectée. Une étude CISAC/PMP Strategy évalue à près de 25% la part des revenus des créateurs menacée d'ici 2028, soit environ 4 milliards d'euros. Depuis janvier dernier, Deezer propose aussi sa technologie de détection à d'autres acteurs du secteur. Des tests concluants ont été menés avec la Sacem, et Billboard l'utilise déjà pour qualifier les titres IA dans ses classements. Vous pouvez d'ailleurs l'utiliser gratuitement sur les autres services de musique en streaming. Une enquête Ipsos menée en 2025 auprès de 9000 personnes dans huit pays indique par ailleurs que 73% des utilisateurs de services de streaming souhaitent savoir si un titre recommandé est entièrement généré par IA.
Deezer reste une application de streaming musical complète pour écouter de la musique et des podcasts sur différents appareils. Son catalogue musical étendu, ses recommandations personnalisées et son système de téléchargement répondent aux usages quotidiens. La version gratuite permet de découvrir le service tandis que l’offre premium améliore sensiblement la qualité d’écoute et le confort d’utilisation. Grâce à ses options audio, à son interface claire et à sa gestion optimisée du streaming en ligne, Deezer constitue une solution fiable pour profiter de chansons et de contenus musicaux à tout moment.

articles.title: Artemis III : la prochaine mission de la Nasa est un véritable cauchemar logistique et technique
articles.text:
Artemis III : la prochaine mission de la Nasa est un véritable cauchemar logistique et technique
Oubliez le schéma classique des missions Apollo. Avant de refouler le sol lunaire, la Nasa prépare pour Artemis III le vol spatial le plus complexe de son histoire. Au programme : 4 astronautes, 3 super-fusées, 3 vaisseaux et un ballet orbital inédit autour de la Terre. Décryptage d'un défi d'ingénierie hors norme.
Lorsque Jared Isaacman, alors nouveau patron de la Nasa, annonça qu'Artemis III ne se poserait finalement pas sur la Lune mais deviendrait une mission de test en orbite terrestre, cela sembla une décision sage et prudente.
Pourtant, à bien regarder les derniers communiqués de l'agence étatsunienne, Artemis III, cette mission d'interopérabilité entre les deux sociétés privées (SpaceX/Blue Origin) et la Nasa, ne présente rien d'autre qu'une complexité jamais vue jusqu'alors.
Artemis 3, 3 fusées, 3 vaisseaux : le défi de la triple synchronisation
Jusqu'ici, l'exploration spatiale habitée reposait sur une certaine simplicité opérationnelle : un seul lanceur géant emportait l'ensemble du matériel. Pour Artemis III, l'agence spatiale américaine casse les codes et prend des risques inédits en articulant sa mission autour de trois lancements distincts depuis la Floride :
- 
Blue Moon Mark 2 (Blue Origin) : déployé en premier par la fusée New Glenn depuis le pas de tir SLC-36 (actuellement détruit suite à l'explosion de la New Glenn 4), cet atterrisseur se placera en orbite basse (LEO) où il pourra patienter jusqu'à 30 jours. 
- 
Orion (Nasa) : propulsé par le géant SLS depuis le pas de tir historique 39B avec les quatre astronautes à bord, il servira de vaisseau central. 
- 
Starship V3 (SpaceX) : propulsé par le booster Super Heavy (depuis le LC-39A ou le SLC-37), il rejoindra l'ensemble dans un second temps. 
Dans l'histoire spatiale, seule la mission soviétique Soyouz T-15 (1986) avait réussi à visiter deux structures distinctes en un seul vol. Mais aligner trois lancements d'engins super-lourds issus d'acteurs publics et privés dans une fenêtre temporelle aussi serrée relève du pur casse-tête opérationnel.
La “Space Coast” au bord de la saturation logistique
Rien que sur Terre, l'enchaînement des tirs va pousser les infrastructures du Cape Canaveral et du centre spatial Kennedy dans leurs derniers retranchements.
Pour réussir ce pari, la Nasa, SpaceX et Blue Origin vont devoir partager des ressources industrielles sous haute tension. Au-delà des créneaux de lancement sur un pas de tir surchargé, c'est toute la chaîne d'approvisionnement en fluides cryogéniques (notamment l'azote gazeux et liquide indispensable aux opérations de préparation) qui sera sous pression. Le moindre pépin technique chez l'un des partenaires menacera de gripper l'ensemble de l'agenda orbital.
Amarrages et tests en vol : deux philosophies d'ingénierie
Une fois les engins calés en orbite terrestre basse, la capsule Orion jouera le rôle de “chasseur” et exécutera une séquence de rendez-vous orbitaux millimétrée.
- 
La phase Blue Origin : Orion viendra s'amarrer sur le flanc du Blue Moon Mk2. Deux astronautes pénétreront dans le module pour valider le système de support de vie (ECLSS), l'avionique et l'ergonomie. Un mannequin de test équipé de la future combinaison lunaire permettra de récolter des données de télémétrie en habitacle. Durant cette opération, c'est Orion qui pilotera l'ensemble. 
- 
La phase SpaceX : après s'être désamarré, Orion rejoindra le gigantesque Starship V3 pour un amarrage frontal (nez à nez). Aucun astronaute n'entrera dans le Starship, le prototype V3 ne disposant pas encore de cabine pressurisée. L'enjeu sera ici informatique et dynamique : tester les communications en direct et le transfert de commandes, le Starship prenant cette fois le contrôle du vol combiné. Contrairement à Artemis IV et les 15 lancements nécessaires de la mégafusée de SpaceX, aucun ravitaillement en orbite n'aura lieu ici. 
Artemis III sera une danse très chorégraphiée avec une séquence de lancement exigeante à travers plusieurs rampes de lancement et des opérations de mission tout aussi exigeantes pour nos équipages de sol et de conduite, ce qui en fait l'une des missions les plus complexes et les plus ambitieuses que la NASA ait jamais entreprises.
En un mot : “Godspeed”
Alors qu'il ne reste plus qu'un an environ avant les trois lancements d'Artemis III, nous sommes forcés de constater que seule une fusée est fonctionnelle : le SLS de la Nasa. La New Glenn a dernièrement explosé avec son pas de tir, et le Starship V3 n'a jamais décollé. Ce sont simplement des faits.
Bien sûr, la grande question que toute la planète du spatial se pose depuis un an, voire plus, est : qui des États-Unis ou de la Chine (re)posera le pied sur la Lune en premier ? Bien malin qui pourrait le dire aujourd'hui. Mais il semble quand même qu'Artemis III sera un vrai tournant : si la mission réussit en temps et en heures, les chances étatsuniennes paraîtront intactes, sinon...

articles.title: The hidden cyber risks facing our water supply
articles.text:
The hidden cyber risks facing our water supply
Our water supply has a big cybersecurity challenge
Cybersecurity risks in water infrastructure have consequences that reach far beyond systems and networks.
Across the sector, the systems responsible for treatment and distribution are becoming more connected. Pumps, sensors and control environments that once operated in isolation are now linked to wider networks, often in the name of efficiency or modernization.
The problem is that these systems were never built with continuous exposure to cyber threats in mind and connecting them has introduced new attack surfaces that are difficult to maintain visibility of and control.
Global Technical Principal, Goldilock Secure.
At the same time, many facilities have crept towards an increasingly blurred line between IT and operational technology (OT). Driven by incremental needs and very practical limits on systemic refresh, these systems have been added to and grown more complex over time rather than being designed securely from the ground up.
As a result, they become more tightly interconnected, with access stretching further across networks and systems than it should. Once an attacker breaches a system, it becomes far easier to move laterally across the network and get closer to critical infrastructure.
Meanwhile, cyber threats continue to encroach on the water sector, with attacks becoming increasingly frequent and their potential impact is hard to ignore. Disruptions to drinking water treatment or control systems can quickly escalate, interrupting supply or affecting water quality and, in turn, the communities that depend on them.
Structural challenges in securing water systems
Securing water infrastructure is made more difficult by the operational realities many providers face. Technology environments have expanded over time, often without dedicated cybersecurity resources growing at the same pace, making it harder to maintain consistent oversight across increasingly ageing and disparate systems.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Many organizations are also balancing modern hyper-connected digital management expectations with the ongoing operation of originally isolated, long-established systems. This places additional pressure on teams responsible for maintaining both resilience and day-to-day continuity.
Another persistent challenge is the divide between IT and operational technology (OT) teams. Because these environments have traditionally evolved separately, with different design approaches, responsibilities, priorities and expertise, they are not always closely aligned, which can slow decision-making and create gaps in visibility during an incident.
In smaller providers, cybersecurity responsibilities may sit with operational staff whose primary expertise lies in running facilities rather than managing cyber risk. Larger organizations may have more specialized cyber teams, but greater separation between functions still introduces coordination challenges and the risk of operational blind spots.
Connectivity without constraint
The growing use of cloud computing platforms and remote access tools has brought clear operational advantages to critical infrastructure like water systems. However, it has also reinforced a default position of keeping systems online at all times, often without a genuine operational imperative for continuous connectivity.
This “always-connected” approach can unnecessarily increase exposure, particularly as more assets become reachable across wider networks. Without clear control over the time windows when systems need to be accessible, organizations may be creating more risk than expected, certainly more than is required.
A stronger, resilient approach starts with recognizing that security grows by making connectivity intentional. Not every system needs to remain online continuously, and limiting unnecessary access significantly improves security outcomes.
This can be achieved by creating stronger separation between critical systems and the wider network, using controls that allow connections to be enabled only when required while maintaining essential operations. In this model, connectivity is actively managed to define resilience on demand.
Containment as a first line of defense
In the event of a vulnerability or compromise, response speed is critical, notably in environments where interconnected systems enable threats to spread rapidly across the network. Without effective connection controls in place, attackers can exploit this unconstrained accessibility to extend their reach before a full response is underway.
The ability to isolate systems in real time helps change this state. Segmenting critical parts of the network helps limit lateral movement, and deeply segmenting down to high criticality digital elements enables organizations to contain threats far more substantially and focus their efforts on speeding up the incident response.
Having this level of control helps limit the spread of disruption and supports a more structured response. It also creates clear, demonstrable evidence of how risk is being managed - something that’s becoming increasingly important as regulatory scrutiny and cyber insurance requirements become more demanding.
Moving to controlled access
The most resilient model possible with physical connection control treats access to critical systems as fully conditional. Rather than keeping them permanently online, connections can be limited to where, when and why they are required for business reasons. As risk levels change, this can be refined or tightened at will.
This lowers both risk and potential impact, minimizing loss, while preserving the flexibility required for day-to-day operations.
For water providers, deliberately managing connectivity and segmenting networks at an infrastructure level should be a priority for resilience. Clearer boundaries and reduced unnecessary access make it easier to protect infrastructure that plays a vital role in public safety.

articles.title: Louer son iPhone au lieu de l'acheter : face à la flambée des prix, Apple s'apprêterait à lancer une offre de leasing
articles.text:
Acheter du matériel Apple coûte sensiblement plus cher depuis quelques semaines. La pénurie mondiale de mémoire a poussé la marque à relever en juin les tarifs de ses ordinateurs et de ses tablettes, parfois de plusieurs centaines d’euros. Plutôt que d’attendre une accalmie qui ne vient pas, Cupertino aurait décidé de revoir la façon dont ses clients paient. Un programme de location baptisé Apple Upgrade serait lancé dès le 28 juillet aux États-Unis, en boutique comme en ligne, avec le suédois Klarna aux manettes.
Comment fonctionnerait cette location d’iPhone à l’américaine ?
Le principe reprend point par point celui de la location automobile. Le client choisit son appareil, passe une rapide vérification de solvabilité gérée par Klarna, puis règle une mensualité fixe. Les iPhone et les Apple Watch se loueraient sur 24 mois, les Mac et les iPad sur 36 mois. À l’échéance, trois portes de sortie : rendre l’appareil, régler le solde pour le garder définitivement, ou basculer vers le modèle suivant, moyennant parfois des frais. Une voiture de fonction, version poche.
Ce dispositif ne viendrait pas compléter l’existant, il le remplacerait. L’iPhone Upgrade Program, lancé en 2015 et jamais proposé en France, cesserait d’accepter de nouveaux inscrits, tout comme les facilités de paiement maison. Le mouvement a d’ailleurs commencé : la version britannique du programme a déjà fermé en janvier dernier. La formule arriverait par ailleurs sans AppleCare+, jusqu’ici inclus dans l’abonnement historique : pendant deux ou trois ans d’engagement, la moindre casse resterait à la charge du locataire. L’entrée de gamme n’a pas droit au ticket non plus : iPhone 16, iPad classique, Apple Watch SE et MacBook Neo sont exclus, au même titre que les entreprises et le secteur éducatif.
Pourquoi maintenant, et surtout, à quand la France ?
L’idée d’un abonnement matériel traîne dans les cartons de Cupertino depuis des années. Un projet interne de souscription, étudié dès 2022, a fini abandonné en 2024 sans jamais voir le jour. Passer par Klarna offre un raccourci commode : le spécialiste du paiement fractionné assume le risque de crédit, Apple garde la vitrine et la relation client.
La flambée des composants a précipité le calendrier. Lancé à 699 € en mars, le MacBook Neo s’affiche à 799 € depuis juin, une hausse de près de 15 % à peine quatre mois après sa sortie. Le MacBook Pro équipé de puce M5 Pro a bondi de 2 549 à 2 949 € dans le même mouvement. Les iPhone ont été épargnés jusqu’ici, mais les nouveaux modèles attendus à la rentrée pourraient alourdir la facture à leur tour.
Vu de France, le mécanisme n’aura pourtant rien d’exotique. Free a ouvert la voie dès 2021 avec Free Flex, une location avec option d’achat sur 24 mois qui propose déjà le même triptyque : rendre, garder ou prolonger. La nouveauté tiendrait à l’identité du loueur : Apple traiterait en direct, sans opérateur ni revendeur entre elle et le client. Le lancement du 28 juillet ne concerne toutefois que les États-Unis, sans calendrier pour l’Europe : les clients français continueront de payer comptant, en plusieurs fois ou via leur opérateur.
