articles.title: Essai du Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 : notre avis sur le téléphone passeport
articles.text:
Au premier contact, le nouveau Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 a tout d’un jouet. À côté de tous les autres smartphones pliants/pliables que j’ai pu tester ces dernières années (tous les Samsung évidemment, sans oublier les Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi ou Google Pixel), le Z Fold 8 est un téléphone minuscule, à qui il semble manquer une partie de son écran, aux dimensions absolument identiques à celles d’un passeport (oui, j’ai comparé les deux). Je n’ai pas encore la certitude qu’il répond à des usages concrets au quotidien, mais je sais après quelques heures d’essai que j’ai envie de l’adopter plus longuement. C’est déjà une première victoire pour Samsung : tous les produits ne font pas cet effet.
Avec le Z Fold 8, Samsung fait le pari d’un très grand écran (7,6 pouces une fois déplié, au format 4:3 utilisable à la verticale ou à l’horizontale) qui peut se ranger dans un gabarit beaucoup plus petit que ses précédents téléphones pliants. Le téléphone est aussi le premier à introduire une dose de silicium-carbone dans la batterie (une première pour Samsung), de la recharge ultra-rapide 45W et un écran Flex Titanium de nouvelle génération conçu pour réduire l’effet du pli. Sur le papier, il a tout d’un produit conçu pour cartonner, et conçu pour réduire le magnétisme d’Apple en septembre avec sa propre version de ce format : avec cette version, les observateurs seront obligés de dire que Samsung est arrivé avant. Notons d’ailleurs que Huawei, avec son Pura X Max, propose un format similaire.
Mignon mais multi-usages : et si Samsung avait trouvé le bon format ?
Contrairement au Z Fold 8 Ultra (le successeur du Z Fold 7), qui a un écran presque carré une fois déplié, le petit Z Fold 8 a l’avantage d’être pensé pour un usage multimédia.
Une fois déplié, son écran est beaucoup plus adapté à une consultation horizontale de vidéo. Mais gare cependant aux bandes noires : en vertical comme en horizontal, le ratio 4:3 ne correspond pas aux usages modernes. C’est mieux que sur les autres pliants, mais pas pour autant parfait. J’avoue avoir été un peu déçu en réalisant qu’un Z Fold 8 Ultra tourné à l’horizontal disposait quasiment du même espace pour une vidéo 16:9 que le Z Fold 8, même si la petite taille du téléphone lui donne un bel avantage. On a dans tous les cas plus d’espace que sur un téléphone « normal ».
Avec seulement 201 grammes sur la balance, le Z Fold 8 a un autre avantage : il est extrêmement pratique à transporter et à manipuler. Samsung adresse ici un marché oublié par les autres marques : les téléphones pliants ont longtemps été considérés comme des briques peu pratiques au quotidien. Avec une épaisseur de 4,5 millimètres une fois déplié et son petit gabarit, le Z Fold 8 offre un confort d’utilisation introuvable ailleurs. C’est aussi pour ça que j’ai beaucoup aimé l’utiliser : le Z Fold 8 me donne l’impression d’utiliser un téléphone d’un nouveau genre, quand les autres pliants me donnent l’impression d’utiliser un téléphone normal qui peut devenir deux fois plus grand.
Sur le reste des caractéristiques, le Z Fold 8 semble irréprochable. Batterie de 4 800 mAh avec du silicium-carbone, puce Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, recharge 45 W séparée en deux pour que chaque batterie reçoive la même puissance… J’ai l’impression que Samsung a pris le Z Fold 8 au sérieux et j’espère qu’Apple fera de même avec son iPhone Fold/Ultra : un téléphone un peu plus petit ne doit pas être moins bon en tout. Le seul vrai bémol ici est l’appareil photo : il n’y en a que deux.
| Z Fold 8 | Z Fold 8 Ultra | |
|---|---|---|
| Écran déplié | 7,6 pouces au format 4:3 | 8 pouces au format 4:3.6 (presque carré) | 
| Écran plié | 5,5 pouces au format 10:16 | 6,5 pouces au format 21:9 | 
| Luminosité | 3000 nits | 3000 nits | 
| Poids | 201 g | 215 g | 
| Épaisseur | 4,5 mm | 4,1 mm | 
| Photo | 50 Mpix + 50 Mpix UGA | 200Mpix + 50 Mpix UGA + 10 Mpix zoom x3 | 
| Puce | Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 | Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 | 
| Stockage | 256 Go, 512 Go et 1 To | 256 Go, 512 Go et 1 To | 
| Batterie | 4800 mAh | 5000 mAh | 
| Charge | 45 W (deux batteries) | 45 W (deux batteries) | 
Un peu de doute sur l’utilisation fermé
Une question reste dans ma tête : plié, au format passeport, le Z Fold 8 est-il vraiment pratique ? Les applications à flux comme Instagram, X ou WhatsApp se consultent verticalement et affichent souvent des listes. En étant moins haut que les autres téléphones, le Z Fold 8 prend le risque de perdre en lisibilité. Faudra-t-il l’ouvrir à chaque fois ? La même question pourra se poser chez Apple en septembre.
Autre interrogation : un peu plus large que les autres téléphones, le Z Fold 8 est pile à la limite du pouce. S’il faut forcément utiliser ses deux mains pour tapoter le clavier, les limites du petit format seront vite trouvées.
Le pli au milieu de l’écran n’a jamais été aussi discret, mais reste un peu présent
L’autre grande innovation de la génération Z Fold 8 est Flex Titanium. Derrière le nom, trois nouvelles pièces glissées sous la dalle : une plaque de titane qui encaisse la pression, une structure en treillis qui la laisse plier au bon endroit et un film d’alliage de titane à peine plus épais qu’un tiers de cheveu. L’ensemble solidifie l’écran, l’amincit de 10 % et s’accompagne d’un nouveau traitement anti-reflet. Je dois reconnaître que j’ai été bluffé : l’écran du Fold 8 fait beaucoup moins plastique, reflète moins la lumière et réduit considérablement la visibilité du pli.
Je veux néanmoins tempérer les annonces de Samsung : sous une lumière vive, le pli réapparaît. Il est bien moins prononcé qu’avant, mais pas encore invisible. Samsung promet surtout que le titane aide l’écran à revenir plus facilement à sa forme d’origine, là où les couches polymères des anciens modèles se déformaient avec le temps et accentuaient la marque. On va espérer que la marque dise la vérité : un Z Fold 8 est très séduisant au déballage, mais le sera-t-il dans 6 mois ?
Rendez-vous bientôt pour notre test complet sur Numerama
Deux heures en main ne suffisent pas pour juger un téléphone comme le Galaxy Z Fold 8 : je vous donne rendez-vous dès maintenant pour un test complet sur Numerama pour trancher sur l’autonomie, la photo, le pli au quotidien et, surtout, l’usage fermé, qui reste ma grande interrogation. Si tout va bien, nous devrions pouvoir vous proposer un test vidéo (YouTube, TikTok et Instagram) et un test écrit dès la semaine prochaine.
Côté prix, le Z Fold 8 démarre à 1 999 euros et le Z Fold 8 Ultra à 2 199 euros (il est un peu plus fin que le Z Fold 7, a le nouvel écran et dispose d’une plus grande batterie, le tout dans le format classique des Fold). Le Z Flip 8, sans évolutions majeures mais avec un design un peu plus fin, débute à 1 299 euros. Tous les tarifs et les offres de précommande peuvent être retrouvés dans notre article dédié.
| 256 Go | 512 Go | 1 To | |
|---|---|---|---|
| Z Fold 8 | 1 999 euros | 2 199 euros | 2 399 euros | 
| Z Fold 8 Ultra | 2 199 euros | 2 399 euros | 2 799 euros | 
Samsung a-t-il trouvé le bon format ? Le Galaxy Z Fold 8 lui permet à la fois de rattraper son retard sur la Chine (batterie silicium-carbone, recharge, technologie d’écran) et d’anticiper l’arrivée d’Apple. Si tout se passe bien, le Galaxy Z Fold 8 a tout d’un futur banger. Reste à savoir si le grand public est prêt à dépenser 2 000 euros pour un téléphone d’un nouveau genre.

articles.title: PC modder bolts 5.5-pound aluminum heatsink to RTX 4060 — convection-only cooling seems to work fine in a testbench-style installation
articles.text:
PC modder bolts 5.5-pound aluminum heatsink to RTX 4060 — convection-only cooling seems to work fine in a testbench-style installation
The size and weight of the card plus the heatsink rivals the hulking RTX 5090 norm.
A PC gamer has DIYed a passive Nvidia GeForce RTX 4060 graphics card system. Perhaps unhappy with the Palit GeForce RTX 3050 KalmX 6GB still being the pinnacle of commercial passive graphics cards in 2026, Bilibili user NexFrame (h/t Fanless Tech) has bolted a hulking finned aluminum heatsink onto an RTX 4060.
NexFrame appears to be a small or up-and-coming ‘brand’ with a penchant for passive PC systems, from what we can understand from their Bilibili bio (machine translation). Unfortunately, we don’t have a lot of information about this passive 5.5-pound (2.5kg) aluminum heatsink-wearing RTX 4060, like whether it is tuned to run cooler than a standard model for fanless operation.
Squinting at the Bilibili video source, a system monitor window seen towards the end of the video appears to show that the GPU is running in a gaming scenario at 58C, with a 71C hotspot. Meanwhile, the graphics fan is running at 0 RPM, which seems accurate. However, the modder doesn’t seem to be taking it easy on the GPU. Further down the system info screen, we see the GPU reportedly pulling 198W. A standard actively cooled RTX 4060 would consume far less than that under load, more like 115W to 120W, so some data must be mangled here, or being misreported.
Elsewhere in the images shared by NexFrame, we can see that the CPU is also being cooled passively. It looks like a hexacore Intel CPU has been combined with a Noctua NH-P1 Passive CPU cooler. This commercial passive cooler was capable of keeping a CPU consuming up to 75W cool and stable enough over extended periods during our review testing. The system monitor tool overlaid on NexFrame’s game testing session shows the CPU sipping between 35 and 50W.
Passively cooled PCs are of interest to a significant number of enthusiasts for eliminating what is typically the noisiest component of a modern PC – fans. In a standard gaming PC, there will be fans built into the CPU cooler, on the GPU shroud, in the PSU, and also arranged at strategic places around the case. Even so-called liquid cooling systems usually rely on their CPU or GPU contact heatsinks being attached to an array of fans cooling a radiator in the case. Just think how blissfully peaceful your computing experience could be if all these moving parts were eliminated.

articles.title: Samsung lance la Galaxy Card, une carte Visa qui offre plus de cashback que l'Apple Card
articles.text:
Une carte bancaire en acier recyclé, également disponible sous forme numérique dans le Samsung Wallet. C’est ce que propose désormais le géant coréen Samsung aux États-Unis, où il vient de lancer sa première carte bancaire pour rivaliser, sur le tard, avec l’Apple Card lancée pour sa part en 2019 sur le même territoire.
Cette annonce intervient chez Samsung à quelques heures de l’ouverture de sa seconde conférence Galaxy Unpacked de l’année, qui a d’ailleurs déjà poussé la firme à sévir contre un journaliste.
Quels avantages pour la Galaxy Card ?
La Galaxy Card fonctionne en l’occurrence sur le réseau Visa, en collaboration avec la banque américaine Barclays.
La Galaxy Card offre à ses utilisateurs des bonus échelonnés : 5% de cashback pour les achats réalisés chez Samsung aux États-Unis, mais aussi 3% de cashback pour les paiements effectués avec la Galaxy Card via le Samsung Wallet, 2% pour les abonnements aux services de streaming et enfin 1% pour tous les autres achats.
À titre de comparaison, l’Apple Card verse 3 % sur les achats réalisés chez Apple, 2 % via Apple Pay et 1 % sur le reste. Sur le papier, la Galaxy Card se montre donc plus généreuse, du moins pour qui reste dans l’écosystème Samsung.
Samsung explique en outre que sa Galaxy Card n’implique aucun frais annuel et que le cashback généré par les différents achats listés plus haut peut être déduit du relevé de la carte de crédit ou transféré sur un compte bancaire.
La Galaxy Card offre enfin quelques avantages complémentaires, comme l’absence de frais de change lors de voyages à l’étranger, la réduction de 20% sur l’adhésion Samsung « VIP Advantage », ainsi qu’un bonus additionnel de 200 dollars (environ 185 €) de cashback si vous dépensez 2000 dollars (environ 1 850 €) au cours des 90 premiers jours d’utilisation de cette nouvelle carte bancaire.
Une carte disponible, mais pas pour nous !
Comme le souligne Neowin, la Galaxy Card peut être utilisée en dehors de l’écosystème de produits Samsung, mais en faisant alors sans le Galaxy Wallet, qui n’est accessible que depuis les montres connectées et les smartphones de la marque. Elle est alors « pilotable » via un portail en ligne de la banque Barclays, avec certaines fonctions en moins.
Autre contrainte, la carte n’est disponible qu’aux États-Unis et pourrait rester un bon moment exclusive à ce marché. Samsung n’exclut pas de proposer sa Galaxy Card dans d’autres pays, mais cette dernière profiterait alors d’avantages radicalement différents et potentiellement moins aguicheurs. C’est d’ailleurs ce qui semble avoir poussé Apple à ne proposer l’Apple Card que sur le marché américain, note WinFuture.
Toutes les annonces de Samsung lors de cette Galaxy Unpacked
La conférence estivale Galaxy Unpacked de Samsung, le constructeur dévoile ses derniers produits en date. Pour suivre la conférence direct, nous vous invitons à suivre notre live écrit.
La conférence de Samsung a lieu ce mercredi 22 juillet depuis 15h.
Pour les smartphones pliables de la marque, ce sont bien trois modèles qui sont dévoilés par le constructeur : le Galaxy Z Fold 8, le Galaxy Z Flip 8 et Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. Vous êtes perdus dans la nouvelle gamme ? Pas de soucis, nous avons défriché les produits tout juste sortis et avons distingué leurs différences.
A cette occasion, nous avons pu prendre en main le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. Sur cette nouvelle gamme, Samsung intègre enfin une batterie silicium-carbone, voici les explications techniques de la marque. Encore une fois, Samsung réalise des prouesses sur son écran. Enfin nous avons fait un comparatif du Z Fold 8 face à notre maquette en impression 3D du futur iPhone pliant.
Du côté des montres connectées, Samsung dévoile deux nouveaux produits : la Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 ainsi que la Galaxy Watch Ultra 2. Notre collègue journaliste Geoffroy a eu l’occasion de tester la Samsung Galaxy Watch 2 Ultra. Vous pouvez aussi lire notre prise en main de la Galaxy Watch 9.

articles.title: Um foguete da SpaceX vai cair na Lua e você poderá ver
articles.text:
Um estágio de foguete abandonado no espaço está em rota de colisão com a Lua. O encontro, previsto para 2026, deve permitir que cientistas acompanhem pela primeira vez detalhes de um impacto artificial no satélite natural.
O objeto pertence a um Falcon 9 da SpaceX e deve atingir a região da Cratera Einstein, no lado visível da Lua, enquanto astrônomos monitoram o fenômeno.
Estágio do Falcon 9 segue em direção à Lua
Segundo estudo, a colisão deve acontecer em 5 de agosto de 2026. O objeto é o estágio superior do foguete Falcon 9, identificado como 2025-010D.
O equipamento foi lançado em janeiro de 2025 para auxiliar o envio de dois módulos robóticos privados ao espaço. Após cumprir sua função, ficou sem combustível e passou a seguir uma trajetória que deve terminar na superfície lunar.
Com cerca de 12 metros de comprimento, 4 metros de largura e aproximadamente 4 toneladas, o estágio deve atingir a Lua a uma velocidade próxima de 8.750 km/h.
Choque deve criar cratera e levantar poeira lunar
Para prever o resultado da colisão, pesquisadores usaram dados calculados pelo astrônomo Bill Grey e simulações de física.
Como o foguete tem uma estrutura metálica oca, a expectativa é que ele seja destruído no impacto, em vez de penetrar profundamente no solo como um asteroide compacto.
As projeções indicam que o evento pode gerar:
- Uma nova cratera com aproximadamente 20 a 30 metros de diâmetro;
- Uma grande nuvem de poeira lunar lançada a vários quilômetros de altura;
- Um clarão visível no momento da colisão;
- Uma nova forma de testar métodos para localizar impactos na Lua.
Astrônomos vão tentar registrar a colisão
Pesquisadores querem que profissionais e astrônomos amadores acompanhem o momento. As imagens podem ajudar a estudar como objetos atingem a superfície lunar e melhorar técnicas usadas em futuras pesquisas.
Leia mais:
- O que aconteceria com nossa mente se vivêssemos na Lua?
- O plano secreto (e bilionário) para transformar a Lua em negócios
- Após Marte, lua de Saturno é discutida como próximo grande destino da exploração humana no espaço
A previsão é que a colisão aconteça às 03h35 no horário de Brasília. Como o choque ocorrerá no lado visível da Lua, será necessário usar câmeras capazes de registrar vídeos em alta velocidade.
Segundo o astrônomo Marcelo Zurita, colunista do Olhar Digital, o impacto poderá ser visto do Brasil e ocorrerá bem próximo da Cratera Carrol, nomeada pela missão Artemis 2.
Entre os sinais esperados estão “o clarão no momento do impacto” e “a pluma de material expelido”.
A queda do estágio do Falcon 9 será uma oportunidade rara para observar um objeto construído pelo ser humano atingindo outro mundo. Além do espetáculo visual, os registros poderão revelar como a superfície lunar reage a esse tipo de choque.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Update für Fritzbox 7510 macht DSL wieder schnell
articles.text:
Probleme mit DSL? Fritzbox-Update macht betroffenen Router wieder schnell
Mit der Fritzbox 7510 hatte Hersteller AVM, der jetzt Fritz heißt, im Jahr 2021 ein DSL-Einstiegsmodell auf den Markt gebracht, das Supervectoring-Anschlüsse mit bis zu 300 Megabit pro Sekunde unterstützt. Zuletzt hatten Nutzer:innen aber über Probleme mit ihrer DSL-Verbindung geklagt.
DSL-Probleme bei der Fritzbox 7510
Demnach soll es in bestimmten technischen Konstellationen dazu gekommen sein, dass Verbindungen unabhängig vom gebuchten Tarif auf maximal zehn Megabit pro Sekunde begrenzt wurden. Die Folge können längere Ladezeiten, langsame Downloads oder Probleme beim Streaming und Online-Gaming sein, wie PC-Welt schreibt.
Mit dem Firmware-Update FritzOS 8.26 für die Fritzbox 7510 soll dieser Fehler jetzt behoben sein. In der entsprechenden Mitteilung geht das Unternehmen auf die Probleme selbst derweil nicht ein. Das Durchführen des Updates wird aber empfohlen, auch weil bei allen Fritzbox-Updates die Sicherheitsfunktionen aktualisiert werden, wie es heißt.
Update behebt Fehler bei DSL-Verbindungen
Neben der Beseitigung der Drosselung auf zehn Megabit pro Sekunde bringt FritzOS 8.26 Verbesserungen der Systemstabilität mit sich. So soll es eine Optimierung von Verbindungen in Mesh-Netzwerken sowie mehr Möglichkeiten im Smart-Home geben. Außerdem bietet die Fritzbox nach dem Update einen Schutz vor dem Ausfall der Internetverbindung. Die Funktion Fritz Failsafe wechselt in diesem Fall automatisch auf eine Ersatzverbindung wie Mobilfunk.
Allerdings sind WLAN-Verbindungen (Wifi 6) bei der Fritzbox 7510 hardwareseitig ohnehin eingeschränkt. Denn das Gerät unterstützt hier ausschließlich das 2,4-Gigahertz-Band. In dicht besiedelten Umgebungen kann das fehlende Fünf-Gigahertz-Band zu Störungen der Verbindung führen, wie Winfuture erklärt.
Aktualisierung über Benutzeroberfläche
Nutzer:innen einer Fritzbox 7510 können das Update über die Benutzeroberfläche der Fritzbox in Gang setzen. Dazu in den Browser „fritz.box“ eingeben und zu „System“ und dort zu „Update“ wechseln. Bei allen Nutzer:innen, die die automatischen Updates aktiviert haben, sollte die Aktualisierung ohne ihr Zutun erfolgen.
Aktuell ist FritzOS 8.26 ausschließlich als Wartungsupdate für die Fritzbox 7510 verfügbar. Es ist allerdings nicht ausgeschlossen, dass weitere Router folgen. Konkrete Informationen dazu gibt es aber noch nicht.

articles.title: Bell touts record-smashing performance following World Cup finale
articles.text:
With the 2026 FIFA World Cup wrapped up, Bell shared details on how its wireless network held up during the event, including the insane amount of data people used.
Bell said that during the 13 matches hosted in Canada (six in Toronto and seven in Vancouver), fans consumed more than 250TB of wireless data across the stadiums, venues, and watch parties, which is about the same as sharing 50 million photos or streaming 83,000 hours of HD video. Bell also carried an additional 80TB of wireless data across official FIFA Fan Festivals and municipal fan zones, bringing total wireless traffic to 330TB.
As a reminder, Bell invested more than $25 million to boost its network’s operations throughout the tournament.
Interestingly, Bell also noted that its command centre operated more than 10 hours per day throughout the tournament, with over 100 Bell employees and 15 external partners supporting the operation.
Switching over to the TV Side, Bell reported that over the 104 tournament matches that took place, it attracted a per-game average of 1.6 million viewers, which is an increase of more than 50 per cent compared to the previous tournament in 2022.
Bell also noted that the final between Spain and Argentina culminated in a record average audience of 6.4 million viewers (up 32 percent compared to 2022), and 14.6 million unique Canadian viewers across TSN, RDS, CTV, Noovo, and Crave. This made it the most-watched FIFA World Cup match ever in Canada, according to Numeris.
As for the Men’s Canadian games, the Round of 16 match vs Morocco attracted an average audience of 5.4 million viewers, which Bell noted was the most-watched match of any non-final ever. Canada’s matches against both Qatar and South Africa also saw similar numbers, reaching both 5.3 million and 5.2 million, respectively.
According to Bell’s press release, Spain vs Argentina, Canada vs Morocco, and Canada vs Qatar were the top three most-watched matches of the whole tournament.

articles.title: Nuevo Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: un formato plegable completamente nuevo y ¿mejor?
articles.text:
Las filtraciones lo adelantaron, y hoy Samsung se ha encargado de confirmarlo en el segundo Unpacked del año. El Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 es oficial. Y, a pesar de no dar pistas en el nombre, se lanza como un modelo completamente nuevo para el catálogo de la compañía. La surcoreana ha querido cambiar su estrategia con dos formatos de 'Fold', y este es el más especial de la nueva generación. Cambia el tamaño, la disposición de la pantalla y acoge un diseño que en China lleva un tiempo con bastante éxito.
La idea de este nuevo Galaxy Z Fold 8 es clara: tener un dispositivo que se adapta a la forma de visualizar contenido en el día a día, haciendo que su pantalla exterior cuente con un formato más cuadrado, mientras que la interior prioriza la reproducción de contenidos en horizontal y mejora el uso de la multiventana.
Samsung lo ha concebido como un nuevo plegable, otra opción más que suma a un catálogo cada vez más completo. Por supuesto, incluyendo en su interior todo lo necesario para sacarle partido, un diseño exterior cuidado y dos de las mejores pantallas del segmento. No sustituye al anterior formato 'Fold': este sigue estando disponible en el también recién presentado Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.
Además, copiando este formato que estrenó Huawei hace un tiempo en el mercado chino, se adelanta a su mayor competidor en Occidente, el futuro iPhone Ultra que, según todas las filtraciones, compartirá este formato más cuadrado cuando esté plegado y más apaisado cuando se despliega.
Nuevo formato sin renunciar a la calidad marca de la casa
El nuevo Galaxy Z Fold 8 se caracteriza por incluir una pantalla exterior en formato 10:16 a la que en Occidente no estamos nada acostumbrados. Ofrece un panel mucho más cuadrado de lo normal, pero que sigue permitiendo utilizar el dispositivo con normalidad gracias a la optimización de One UI 9. Todo está más achatado y girar el dispositivo en modo apaisado pierde algo de valor, pero por un motivo más que obvio.
Cuando lo despliegas, ahora no tienes una pantalla cuadrada: su formato es 4:3 en formato horizontal, un panel muchísimo más recomendable para jugar o ver vídeos sin las ya clásicas franjas negras que se acostumbran en los Fold de generaciones anteriores. A modo de resumen, un móvil para quien utiliza el formato plegable priorizando el contenido audiovisual y los juegos.
El nuevo formato no renuncia a lo que venía haciendo Samsung: ambos paneles son Dynamic AMOLED 2X, tienen resoluciones más allá del FullHD y cuentan con la tecnología adaptativa de Samsung que permite ir de 1 hasta 120 Hz dependiendo del uso que hagas de la pantalla en cada momento.
En el caso de la exterior, estamos ante un panel de 5,5 pulgadas que promete un dispositivo compacto cuando está plegado. En su defecto, cuando se despliega, se revela un panel de 7,6 pulgadas en formato 4:3 y un pliegue que, según Samsung, está mucho más trabajado para que apenas se note.
Todo, en un conjunto con unas dimensiones bastante compactas que recuerdan más a un Flip que a un Fold: este Galaxy Z Fold 8 pesa 201 gramos y tiene un grosor de 9,7 mm. Además, por supuesto, de contar con cuerpo completamente metálico en los bordes y un cristal con textura mate en la trasera.
El Galaxy Z Fold 8 tampoco se olvida del rendimiento y apuesta por una batería contundente
Samsung ha hecho dos cosas muy bien con este Galaxy Z Fold 8. Para empezar, ha incluido en su interior el mejor procesador del momento. Es el Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy, un chip con el que todo vuela, con una gran optimización energética y mucho potencial IA para sacarle partido a las ventajas de Galaxy AI.
La compañía tampoco escatima en memorias: el Galaxy Z Fold 8 llega con 12 o 16 GB de RAM y tres versiones de almacenamiento: 256 GB, 512 GB o 1 TB. En otras palabras: la combinación perfecta entre RAM, almacenamiento y procesador para que todo vaya a la perfección.
Y, si bien esta decisión no es muy sorprendente en los móviles de gama alta de Samsung, lo que la compañía ha hecho con la batería de este Galaxy Z Fold 8 sí es motivo de sorpresa. Ha incluido en su interior una celda de 4.800 mAh que, si bien no es la más grande vista en un plegable, supone una actualización importante respecto a los modelos del año pasado. El Z Fold 7 cuenta con 4.400 mAh siendo más grande y pesado.
También hay alegrías en otro apartado clave: los Fold este año cargan a 45 W por cable y 20 W de forma inalámbrica. Según Samsung, podrás recargar el 63% de su batería en solo 30 minutos.
El nuevo formato trae de la mano un recorte en la cámara
La nueva estrategia de diseño nos deja con un recorte en el apartado de cámara. Este nuevo Galaxy Z Fold 8 no incluye un sensor teleobjetivo como sí veíamos en generaciones anteriores del modelo Fold. La compañía este año ha llevado esta opción únicamente al Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, haciendo que este modelo esté más cerca del Flip cuando se trata de hacer fotos y grabar vídeo.
En la cámara trasera, el Galaxy Z Fold 8 tiene dos sensores y ambos son de 50 MP. El principal es un viejo conocido de la marca con una apertura f/1.8, OIS y una resolución suficiente para disparar con un zoom de dos aumentos (2x) y mantener una "calidad óptica". El segundo sensor es el ya clásico ultra gran angular f/1.9 con un FOV bastante amplio de 120°.
Ahora bien, como nos tienen acostumbrados los Fold, hay dos cámaras más de las que debes dar cuenta. Ambas son prácticamente idénticas: dos sensores selfie de 10 MP colocados, uno en la pantalla exterior y otro en la interior.
Es un conjunto de cámaras que se sitúa por debajo de lo que nos venía acostumbrando Samsung en los Fold de turno, pero que sale del paso en un formato más destinado al consumo de contenido que a la creación del mismo. Palabras, por otro lado, que no dejan a este dispositivo mal posicionado en el ámbito fotográfico, pero que le dan al usuario un aliciente para ir a por el modelo Ultra en caso de necesitar los 200 MP o el sensor teleobjetivo.
| Características | Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 | 
|---|---|
| Pantalla interior | 7,6 pulgadas Resolución QXGA+ (1.848 x 2.448) Dynamic AMOLED 2X Tasa de refresco adaptativa (1-120 Hz) Vision Booster | 
| Pantalla exterior | 5,5 pulgadas Resolución WUXGA++ (1.248 x 1.972) Dynamic AMOLED 2X Tasa de refresco adaptativa (1-120 Hz) Vision Booster | 
| Procesador | Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 | 
| Memorias | 12 o 16 GB de memoria RAM 256 GB, 512 GB o 1 TB de almacenamiento | 
| Cámaras | Sensor principal de 50 MP: Dual Pixel AF, OIS, F1.8, tamaño de píxel: 1.0μm, FOV: 85 Sensor ultra gran angular de 50 MP: Quad Pixel AF, F1.9, tamaño de píxel: 0.7μm, FOV: 120˚ Cámara selfie exterior de 10 MP: F2.2, Tamaño de píxel: 1.12μm, FOV: 100˚ Cámara selfie interior de 10 MP: F2.2, Tamaño de píxel: 1.12μm, FOV: 85˚ | 
| Batería y carga | Batería de 4.800 mAh Carga por cable de 45 W Carga inalámbrica de 20 W | 
| Otros | WiFi 7 Bluetooth 6.0 5G Protección IP48 Android 17 y One UI 9 | 
| Dimensiones | Plegado: 81.9 x 123.9 x 9.7 mm Desplegado: 161.4 x 123.9 x 4.5 mm Peso: 201 gramos | 
| Precio | Desde | 
Precio y disponibilidad del Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8
Este Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 se acaba de presentar en sociedad durante el Unpacked junto con el Galaxy Z Flip 8 y el Galaxy Z Fold Ultra, tres dispositivos que ya están disponibles para reservar en la web de Samsung y otros distribuidores.
Se pondrán a la venta el 7 de agosto y, en el caso concreto del Galaxy Z Fold 8, hay cuatro versiones de color disponibles: grafito, blanco, lavanda y pistacho (este último, exclusivo solo en la web de Samsung). ¿Su precio? Aquí tienes las cifras para las diferentes versiones de almacenamiento y RAM.
- Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 | 12 GB + 256 GB: 1.999 euros.
- Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 | 12 GB + 512 GB: 2.199 euros.
- Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 | 16 GB + 1 TB: 2.599 euros.
Samsung está ofreciendo descuentos y bonificaciones especiales por tiempo limitado, pudiendo obtener hasta 896 euros para la compra de un nuevo plegable a través del programa Entrega y Estrena. A esto se suman 100 euros de descuento directo con Entrega y Estrena y 150 euros de descuento adicional si se paga con PayPal.

articles.title: The Download: NASA’s new space telescope and OpenAI’s autonomous hacker
articles.text:
The Download: NASA’s new space telescope and OpenAI’s autonomous hacker
Plus: France has become the first EU country to ban social media for under-15s.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Shape-shifting mirrors on NASA’s new space telescope could unveil Jupiters like our own
When NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launches, as early as the end of next month, it will attempt one of astronomy’s most precise disappearing acts to date. It will carry the first space-bound “active” coronagraph, an instrument that effectively erases most of the light from a star during photography.
The technology will allow astronomers to take the first pictures of planets orbiting other stars that are similar to those in our solar system. Ultimately, it could pave the way for a future mission that could snap the first photos of Earth-like worlds.
“I hope it’s remembered for it being that critical stepping stone for … finding Earth 2.0,” says Brandon Creager, the instrument’s lead mechanical engineer.
Read the full story on the space telescope that could transform the search for distant planets.
—Eshan Raul
MIT Technology Review Narrated: PsiQuantum has a plan to make a massive quantum computer out of light
The machine that could change the world will be housed in a room that looks like a data center crossed with an ice cream factory.
Inside, some 100 stainless-steel cabinets each hold hundreds of chips. On those chips, thousands of light particles will fly through a maze of optical switches and beam splitters. Each photon must be accounted for, because precisely measuring where it ends up will help answer questions that current computers might take millions of years to solve.
This computer, as described, does not exist. It’s the brainchild of a company called PsiQuantum, founded in 2016 by four physicists from UK universities. In a crowded field of deep-pocketed competitors with similarly fantastical visions, the company aims to be the first to build a useful quantum machine.
—James O'Donnell
This is our latest story to be turned into an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotifyand Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 OpenAI says one of its models carried out an autonomous hack
It escaped its testing sandbox and breached AI research platform Hugging Face. (Reuters $)
+ OpenAI described it as a cybersecurity test that went badly wrong. (WSJ $)
+ The hack is among the first known cyberattacks by an AI acting on its own. (FT $)
+ Even simple AI attacks are cause for alarm, though. (MIT Technology Review)
2 France has become the first EU country to ban social media for under-15s
Its parliament approved the ban, which President Macron championed. (NYT $)
+ He pledged to enforce it by September, the start of the school year. (Guardian)
+ But critics say it’s unconstitutional and impossible to enforce. (NPR)
3 The US and China will hold talks over AI in September
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will lead the US side. (Reuters $)
+ Chinese models have Trump’s AI world at war with itself. (MIT Technology Review)
4 Publishers are considering cutting Google off as AI reshapes search
News outlets are weighing lost traffic against AI exposure. (WSJ $)
5 Samsung is in talks to invest €1 billion in Mistral
The French AI firm is positioning itself as an alternative to US models. (FT $)
+ It’s Europe's leading AI firm, but US peers dwarf its $20 billion valuation. (Reuters $)
6 Amazon pushed up rivals’ prices, leaked records allege
Internal emails reveal tactics that allegedly reshaped online pricing. (Guardian)
7 Trump has tapped a Big Tech critic to lead the DOJ's antitrust division
Adam Candeub has called for tougher federal competition enforcement. (FT $)
8 New drilling methods could unlock geothermal energy almost anywhere
They aim to unlock Earth’s enormous heat reserves. (New Scientist $)
+ AI is uncovering hidden geothermal energy resources. (MIT Technology Review)
9 AI researchers have proposed a “Genie coefficient” for measuring AI risks
It would track the gap between intent and action. (IEEE Spectrum)
+ We need better ways to evaluate AI. (MIT Technology Review)
10 Japan's AI boom has two unlikely winners: a toilet maker and an MSG giant
They’re supplying critical chipmaking materials. (CNBC)
Quote of the day
“He’s an analog man in a digital AI world, and I think that’s incredibly appealing.”
—Paul Dergarabedian, a movie industry analyst at Comscore, tells Fortune that Christopher Nolan’s commitment to human filmmaking provides an attractive counterweight to Hollywood’s embrace of AI.
One More Thing
Taiwan’s “silicon shield” could be weakening
  Taiwan produces the majority of the world’s semiconductors and more than 90% of the most advanced chips needed for AI applications. Many believe that’s helped deter China from invading the island. But now some Taiwan specialists and citizens are worried that this “silicon shield” is cracking.
Facing pressure from Washington, TSMC—the world’s largest chipmaker—is expanding manufacturing abroad. In Taiwan, there are worries that this will dilute the company’s power at home, making the US and other countries less inclined to defend the island.
Find out why Taiwan's chipmaking dominance could be key to its future security.

articles.title: Microsoft is bringing original Xbox games to PC
articles.text:
Microsoft is expanding its Xbox backward compatibility efforts today by bringing original Xbox games to PC. An early preview release will see four classic Xbox games available on PC today, as part of a bigger effort to bring more Xbox console games to PC in the future.
Microsoft is bringing original Xbox games to PC
Xbox backward compatibility for PC allows classic Xbox console games to officially run on Windows.
Xbox backward compatibility for PC allows classic Xbox console games to officially run on Windows.
The first four games are Blinx: The Time Sweeper, Conker: Live and Reloaded, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge, and Fuzion Frenzy. You’ll be able to purchase and download each of these games on PC, and they’ll also be included with all Xbox Game Pass plans. If you already own a digital copy of these games, you can now play them on PC or handhelds like the Xbox Ally and Xbox Ally X.
Microsoft has also added a bunch of PC features to these games to make it easier to customize graphics settings while maintaining the original gameplay. VSync support has been added, alongside up to 4x resolution upscaling, anisotropic filtering, enhanced anti-aliasing, fullscreen and windowed modes, and more.
Achievements are also coming to these four classic Xbox games in the coming months, a highly requested addition for both console and PC. All four titles will also include customizable language and audio settings.
Most modern PCs will be able to run these Xbox games comfortably, and Microsoft’s minimum system requirements include:
- GPU: Nvidia GTX 950 or AMD Radeon RX 550 or Intel UHD 770 or Intel Arc A310
- CPU: Intel Core i3-8100 or AMD Ryzen 3 1200 or AMD Ryzen Z2 A Processor
- RAM: 8GB
You will also need Windows 11 to run these original Xbox games, and Microsoft recommends a GTX 1070 Ti or equivalent on the GPU side and a six-core CPU like the Intel Core i5-10400 or AMD Ryzen 5 3600 to get the best out of these games.
“This marks the beginning of a broader effort to preserve Xbox games from the past and bring them to PC over time,” says Jason Ronald, VP of next generation at Xbox. “Xbox Backward Compatibility on PC is another step toward preserving the games from the past and making it easier for you to enjoy and play more of the games you already own across the devices you use every day.”
Ronald first teased that classic Xbox games were coming to PC earlier this year, in a discussion about the next-generation Project Helix Xbox console. Microsoft’s next Xbox will also play PC games, and the company has been working on a disc-to-digital feature that will allow Xbox owners to digitize their existing physical game collections in preparation for future Xbox consoles.

articles.title: Dimension Capital's $800M third fund shows the intersection of science and compute is booming | TechCrunch
articles.text:
While many newer VC firms are still struggling to raise fresh capital, Dimension Capital, founded in late 2022, has been raising increasingly larger funds in quick succession. On Tuesday, the New York firm — which invests at the intersection of science and compute — announced an $800 million fund, which is 60% larger than its $500 million second vehicle announced just 18 months ago.
When Zavain Dar and Adam Goulburn — formerly partners at Lux Capital — teamed up with Obvious Ventures alum Nan Li to launch the firm four years ago, they bet that founders would increasingly want to build deep-tech companies that crossed the boundaries of biotech and software. Now, the three partners admit to being impressed by how quickly their thesis has played out.
In 2024, they co-led a $30 million seed investment in Chai Discovery. The startup, which is developing open source AI foundation models for drug development, announced last week that it raised $400 million at a $3.8 billion valuation. The firm also backed anti-aging startup New Limit at its Series A round in January 2025. Earlier this month, New Limit, co-founded by Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong, completed a Series C at a $3.1 billion valuation.
The firm’s other notable investments include inference company Modal Labs and Anthropic. Dimension received shares in the AI giant after Anthropic acquired its portfolio company, the drug discovery platform Coefficient Bio, this spring for a reported $400 million.

articles.title: Thermalright Launches Royal Pretor 130 Vision CPU Cooler
articles.text:
Tuesday, July 21st 2026
	
	
	
	Thermalright Launches Royal Pretor 130 Vision CPU Cooler
Thermalright today launched the Royal Pretor 130 Vision, a high-end CPU air cooler. The cooler features a large, dual fin-stack (D-type) heatsink with a pair of fans in push-pull configuration, and is characterized by a top-plate that features a 3.95-inch true-color display. The cooler's construction involves a nickel-plated copper base, from which six copper heatpipes pass through, conveying heat to the cooler's two fin stacks. A combination of a 130 mm and 120 mm fan ventilate the heatsink. The heatsink measures 130 mm x 140 mm x 165 mm (WxDxH), including its fans in place. The company didn't reveal weight.
The 3.95-inch color LCD comes with a 480 x 480 pixels resolution, and uses a 9-pin USB 2.0 header for both power and display connectivity. The included software lets you put out system monitoring pulled from ACPI, or just about anything. The 130 mm fan included is the Thermalright TL-HD13-X28. It is 28 mm-thick, and features an S-FDB V2 bearing, taking in 4-pin PWM connection. It turns at speeds of up to 1,750 RPM, pushing up to 81.88 CFM of airflow at up to 2.38 mm H₂O static pressure, and up to 28.3 dBA of noise. The 120 mm fan located between the two fin-stacks is the Thermalright TL-H12-X28-R9, a 28 mm-thick spinner that turns at up to 2,400 RPM, pushing up to 98.2 CFM of airflow at 2.48 mm H₂O static pressure, and 32.7 dBA noise output. Much like its 130 mm neighbor, it features a second generation S-FDB bearing. The company didn't reveal pricing.

articles.title: From Highways To Health Care: Portability Proves Key To Physical AI
articles.text:
Success at the edge takes advantage of common threads — lithography, imaging, chiplets, and AI.
Key Takeaways:
With a healthy boost from AI and high-performance compute, medical devices, electric vehicles, and humanoid robots enabled by semiconductor technology today are poised to transform lifestyles tomorrow. To accomplish this goal, engineers are leveraging commonalities across disparate applications to achieve economies of scale across many industries and make chiplet commercialization feasible.
As portability efforts increase, companies are taking co-development among partners to new levels to surmount the challenges of sub-2nm. Nowhere is this more important than in advanced lithography.
Increasing die size drives reticle stitching solutions
With considerable engineering effort, existing tools often can be used to address entirely new problems. For instance, the lithography exposure field is limited by the reticle size (26 x 33 mm). That limits the size of modern chips, which is especially important for SoCs. The solution to date has been to divide functionality among chiplets, breaking down the SoC into smaller chip sizes.
A competing approach is to stitch two adjacent fields together by running patterns across the edge of the reticle, forming one chip across both fields. “There’s a lot of technical complexities with stitching, because you’re now introducing these borders between patterns on your chip. The field edge introduces significant distortion, which affects imaging,” explains Germain Fenger, senior director of product management at Synopsys. “Normally, we ignored this because it’s at the edge of the die, but now the edge has made it to the middle, so part of this involves modifying the design to optimize routing placement across the fields.”
Leading chipmakers already use inverse lithography technology (ILT) and optical proximity correction (OPC) at the most critical exposure layers at 5nm and beyond. ILT is a computationally intensive process, with long write times, that produces curved features on the mask. This process accounts for the distortions introduced by the optics and process variations, resulting in straight lines on the wafer.
“We also may modify design rules locally, if they need to be modified,” said Fenger. “Basically, it’s a combination of OPC and ILT that enables the best lithographic performance, and at imec we can validate our tools for this difficult patterning challenge. Imec is also the perfect environment to think outside the box to see not just how we can do more of the same, but maybe do something different in the flow to solve this challenge.”
Automotive through vertical integration
One of the most significant trends in the automotive industry is the shift from older-node chips to leading-edge processes, particularly for ADAS and autonomous capabilities.
“The semiconductors used in a vehicle are very, very diverse,” said Vidya Rajagopalan, senior vice president of electrical hardware at Rivian. “We have high-performance application processors, we have real-time processors that are very reliant on being jitter-free, we have cellular modems, we have RF performance, we have GNSS, and we have electromechanical products, mechatronic products, displays, audio, speakers.”
Fig. 1: Vertical integration simplified the electronics to just a handful of PCBs. Source: Rivian
Rivian’s first-generation in-house autonomy processor, RAP1, is a custom 5nm SOC from TSMC that is integrated with three HBM stacks. Interestingly, the company is able to use virtually the same hardware platform, broken into three to five zonal PCBs for all its vehicles, trucks, and delivery vans. “By 2030, about 50% of the car’s bill of materials will be electronics, which also reflects the growing software complexity that comes with the modern vehicle.”
Rivian took a vertically integrated approach to EV design, simplifying the electronic content. “Until recently, most OEMs acted as integrators of units purchased from Tier One suppliers, and the Tier One suppliers all specialized in different things,” Rajagopalan said. “As a result, the vehicle contained 40 to 100 electronic control units. We had the luxury of looking at this as a clean sheet of paper, so we see our vehicle as one large network computer. We design nearly all the electronics, which is much simpler. Only two companies in the western hemisphere have done this, along with a bunch of companies in China.”
Fig. 2: Under the hood of the MCMs sit leading-node SoCs surrounded by HBMs. Source: Rivian
That will likely change. “You’re going to see far more sophisticated packages in automotive, much more complicated multichip modules — memory, SoCs, and power management,” she said. “A lot of people talk about determinism and low latency in physical AI, but we assume these in a self-driving car.” The company’s third-generation technology and vehicles are due out later this year.
Using co-development, but kicking it up a notch
Co-development is not a new concept in the industry, but it’s being taken to new levels to meet the stringent performance specifications of sub-5nm devices and chiplet-based packaging. “At advanced nodes, performance is no longer driven by single steps, but by the interaction between processes such as bonding, thinning, CMP, and packaging,” said Douglas Guerrero, senior technologist at Brewer Science. “Together with imec and its partners, materials can be tested across full process flows rather than isolated steps, improving robustness.”
For example, one imec collaboration with Brewer’s scientists resulted in a commercial-ready material platform that meets tighter performance specifications for thermal stability, adhesion, and ultraclean debond with reduced process variability, all of which enabled faster adoption in manufacturing. “Without imec, the project likely would have taken longer due to limited access to integrated process flows and cross-industry feedback loops.”
One base technology, dozens of applications
Several examples show how base technologies can be adapted to multiple uses, such as optical filters deposited on CMOS image sensors that enable hyperspectral imaging. Hyperspectral imaging can help preserve healthy tissue during surgery, ensure the freshness of food, optimize water use in crop fields, detect blood or gunpowder at crime scenes, or separate plastics for automated recycling, among several other uses.
Hyperspectral imaging captures the signature of materials from close-up, as in identifying layers in antique oil paintings. From great distances, compact cameras can be fitted on drones for everything from warfare to determining exactly which crops need watering.
This imaging technology is built on commercial CMOS image sensors. “The filter is made up of a lot of flat thin layers that make the transmission peaks, so they have spectral responses we design them for. By choosing different materials and different thicknesses, we can simulate what the total transmission will be,” explained Tina Babu Shylaja, R&D engineer at imec. Many filters can be integrated and aligned with lithographic precision to individual pixels with a pitch of ~5 μm. A wet cavity etch creates a staircase over the pixel array, allowing each step to act as an independent optical filter while the thickness of the transparent cavity determines the central wavelength of the filter.
Breakthrough medical devices
imec researchers are developing a variety of medical devices designed to replace more risky techniques already in use. “We are focusing our research on using neuromodulation implants to address chronic problems like essential tremor or depression,” said Milind Pandit, an imec R&D engineer. “We focus on vagus nerve stimulation or deep brain stimulation using ultrasound. The reason we use ultrasound rather than electrical stimulation with probes is that ultrasound is a bit more versatile in steering waves to specific points in the brain. That is important because research on the brain is still up and coming, which means people are not completely aware of the mechanisms and the areas of stimulation that lead to certain results. Furthermore, scar tissue doesn’t form, because you’re not actually penetrating the brain tissue. It is only from the surface of the structure, so somatosensory problems due to the waves reflecting back from the skull do not come into play.”
One hyperspectral imaging application that has received FDA clearance in the U.S. is used for open and minimally invasive surgical applications. “The surgeon wants to remove all the unhealthy region, while sparing as much healthy tissue as possible,” said Josh Gibson, head of technology at Hypervision Surgical. “Crucially, you need to cut where there is still sufficient blood flow, then stitch it back together so that you have blood flow across that joint for good healing.”
The hyperspectral camera detects oxygen saturation levels in tissue and may help identify tissue at risk from ischemia. That allows for maximum preservation of healthy tissue.
Yet another exciting area is hyperspectral imaging of the retina of the eye to provide early-stage diagnosis of signatures for brain conditions, including Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and Huntington’s diseases. Because these typically are diagnosed after onset, the idea of this imaging is to have a non-invasive method of identifying the signature associated with each disease before symptoms appear.
Interestingly, using AI in medicine can mean a variety of breakthroughs even without introducing any new technologies or instruments. “It’s pretty extraordinary that most measurements in health undergo some form of wave-forming compression, and because of that compression, we are often losing the medically relevant data that we want based on either human perception or human values that we want to collapse that data into,” said Dan Wattendorf, director of Accelerator Global Health at the Gates Foundation. “When we look at the initial ML and transformer-based AI learning models just on the waveforms of an EKG, we’re starting to see astonishing things that no clinician or cardiologist can see. Embedded in that data, you can see whether someone had atrial fibrillation a decade ago. We can see structural heart defects that are only seen on ultrasound in the EKG signal.”
Wattendorf explained that compression of data is even more dramatic in a CBC (complete blood count) reading where 9 million data points are compressed to about 20 numbers viewed by the physician. In tracking 12,000 healthy patients over a 20-year period, Mass General Brigham Hospital showed that individuals whose data fall within specification levels can have very different distributions and setpoints, resulting in no detection of strong variance outside of one’s baseline. “This is clear to any data scientist, but we need to have access to that data. We haven’t even begun to look at the uncompressed data behind these medical waveforms.”
Humanoid robots 
There is an argument for reusing some technology even in something as new as humanoid robots. “In talking to developers of humanoid robots, they emphasize they cannot afford to rewrite the compute stack for each of their robots. Determinism, openness, and scalability are the driving forces behind physical AI architectures, not peak TOPS,” said Salil Raje, senior vice president and general manager of AMD’s adaptive and embedded computing group. “Such a system has a brain that is doing the perception, planning, and decision-making, and it’s running large language models. The spine in the middle is a synchronous fabric that connects up most of the nodes. This is typically run on time-sensitive networks. It has one global clock, and it aligns all the nodes to within microsecond latencies. And then you have the body — hundreds of sensors that are fusing data from vision, from audio, from motors, with forces and inertia data. The limb controllers are doing the slacks and safety moves, and then you have the joint and the motor controls doing the torque and actuation.”
To meet latency requirements, Raje said that meeting real-time response requires data to be maintained locally. “You encode the data, you filter the data, you resize the data, and you send only insights, tokens, metadata to the central brain, and that enables a two to three orders of magnitude of improvement in data traffic.”
Efficiency and reliability rule in physical AI
Sensing data is critical in physical AI, but it needs to be energy-efficient. “We can leverage bio-inspired technologies for edge AI to improve efficiency,” said Ahmed Bahai, chief technology officer at Texas Instruments. “For instance, our brains are processing data in a very different way, a much more efficient way than current devices. In fact, you can debate whether its capacity is 1016 FLOPs (floating point operations per second), or 1015, but that doesn’t matter. What matters is that the efficiency of our brains is about 10,000 times greater than anything we have produced today. And it does not use an LLM, but an SLM (sensory language model). Even a baby learns languages from a few words and then uses intuition to build their vocabulary. So there is a lot we can learn when power is at stake, because today’s devices are more power-limited than transistor-limited.”
This core focus on energy efficiency will be a must for generative AI and physical AI acceptance, especially among the general population.
Progress from automotive informs everything autonomous
At its International Technology Forum (ITF), imec announced that it renamed the Autonomous Edge Chiplet Program (AECP), which builds on the foundational expertise and technology approaches of the Automotive Chiplet Program (ACP), launched in 2024. To date, the ACP has assembled 24 members, including OEMs, Tier 1 suppliers, IC manufacturers, EDA companies, and OSATs. A separate program helped catalyze CHASSIS (Chiplet-based Hardware Architectures for Software-defined Vehicles), which grew out of the ACP as a joint European project led by Bosch.
“We just opened our new site in Heilbronn in Germany, a chiplet acceleration center that is designed to bridge the gap between research and industrialization. The center has one goal — to really focus on prototyping — driving compliance and making sure that we’re de-risking prioritization of chiplets for the automotive industry,” said Dieter Hoffend, director of business development for AECP.
Fig. 3: The ACP is global, bringing together OEMs, Tier 1 suppliers, semiconductor manufacturers, EDA firms and OSATs. Source: imec
Portability from the CHASSIS hardware/software reference platform to similar platforms is another goal. “There is a common architectural DNA within chiplets that scales across multiple industries,” said Hoffend. “It has to do with compute, AI, safety, memory, and scalability. All of the same kinds of challenges that we are addressing in the ACP apply to the AECP. What differs is certainly the specifications associated with those vertical segments, and as such you may see different I/Os, different sensing applications, etc. But we truly believe that the core of what we do in automotive will be scalable into other segments. Reusing architectures will reduce the cost and accelerate time to market.”
Hoffend emphasized how important this shared expertise is. While 96.4 million vehicles were manufactured in 2025, volumes for individual vehicles remain fairly flat from year to year compared to those found in consumer electronics. “Automotive is a relatively small market from a semiconductor perspective. So how do we reconcile exponential compute demand with linear market economies? We at imec believe chiplets are the answer.”
Fig. 4: The chiplet-based reference design for physical AI will take foundational learning from the ACP and form an architectural foundation for humanoid robots, drones, and industrial automation. Source: imec
The group has set a 12-month deadline to build a reference platform for edge applications, prioritizing interoperability among chiplets from multiple vendors and hardware/software co-design. He added that the Automotive Chiplet Program is not confined to EU member states, and that imec is working with Japan’s Advanced SoC Research for Automotive (ASRA) to harmonize the standardization of chiplet architectures for automotive applications. The organizations have agreed to jointly explore and promote shared architecture specifications.
Conclusion
For all the disruption, it’s important to remember that much of the progress made on the technology front is being layered atop existing platforms, methods, and techniques that have worked in the past. That includes co-development agreements between companies such as imec, Fraunhofer Institute, and CEA-Leti, along with suppliers, chipmakers, and end customers.
Large challenges — like making stitching work across reticle fields, or making chiplet platforms compatible with products from different vendors — will require the closest of partnerships and collaborative thinking. Multiple solutions will be needed, and no single company can solve the challenges of sub-2nm processing and advanced packaging alone.

articles.title: Cyber criminals targeting familiar systems of our digital life to run their scams - Tech Guide
articles.text:
New research from Gen, parent company of internet security company Norton, has uncovered some alarming news showing cyber criminals infiltrating systems people trust to run their scams and steal your money.
Gen’s H1 2026 threat report showed the latest threats had one thing in common – they were moving away from sending malicious links or dropping malware and instead targeting familiar systems and workflows we use every day.
In Australia scams were the biggest threat in the first half of 2026, followed by phishing, malvertising, and scam yourself attacks.
Scam activity has spiked by 32 per cent with a sharp rise in gambling scams, which surged an incredible 927 per cent while e-shop scams rose by 76 per cent, tech support scams were up 68 per cent, dating scams up 31 per cent and generic financial scams up 70 per cent.
But the central finding of the threat report shows a definitive shift in how attacks are launched.
The most successful threats in the first half of the year didn’t rely on technical exploits or deception.
Instead they succeeded because they were hard to tell apart from normal digital life.
For example a scam arrives through a hotel booking platform referencing a real reservation.
Or WhatsApp accounts compromised not through a password breach but by tricking users into approving an attacker’s browser as a linked device.
Fraud has also moved through real and verified financial accounts because the people behind those accounts had been recruited through social media with offers of quick cash.
“The most effective attacks in the first half of 2026 didn’t look like attacks,” said Vita Santrucek, Chief Technology & Development Officer at Gen.
“They arrived through booking platforms, family message threads, software update channels and AI agent workflows – all places people already trust.
“As attackers blend into everyday digital experiences, protection has to move closer to the moments where confidence is earned, exploited or broken.”
Threat Report Highlights
– 114.2 million e-shop scam attacks blocked, up 109 per cent – highlighting the growing risk of fake online stores targeting shopper
– A 387 per cent increase in government impersonation scams – showing criminals are increasingly exploiting trust in public institutions to steal money and information
– A more than 454 per cent increase in family impersonation scams, while separate “GhostPairing” activity showed how WhatsApp’s linked-device feature can be abused to gain persistent access to an account and allow people to impersonate loved ones
– 20.3 million tech support scam attacks blocked – reflecting continued attempts to trick people into giving scammers remote access to their devices or financial information
– More than 304 million scam-ad impressions identified across the EU and UK in less than one month – underscoring how easily fraudulent ads can reach people
– Roughly 1.9 billion tracking attempts blocked during H1 2026 – demonstrating the scale of online tracking that can erode consumer privacy
– Norton and LifeLock breach notification alerts with attributed lead sources increased 628.1 per cent up to 3.3 million, with more than 10 million breach notifications sent in total – proving more people’s personal information is being exposed in data breaches
– 734 per cent increase in bank account (depository) activity alerts – further evidence of the rapid financial exploitation that follows a breach
– 1 million web skimming attacks blocked, up 212 per cent – showing how attackers continued to target checkout flows where users already expect to enter payment details
– More than 15.7 million breached records containing email addresses identified, giving cybercriminals more opportunities to target consumers with phishing, scams, and account takeover attempts

articles.title: This Nigerian founder has built AI-powered tools in the agri, ed-tech spaces - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian founder Juliet Chinenye Duru has designed and built two AI-powered tools from the ground up to solve real, tangible problems she observed in the Nigerian and African context.
AgriAI gives smallholder farmers a region-specific crop yield prediction and a concrete actionable recommendation, running on a cheap Android phone over a standard 3G connection.
NaijaLearn-AI, meanwhile, is a free multilingual AI tutor covering STEM and ICT topics in English, Pidgin, Yoruba, Hausa, and Igbo, accessible to students across all 250 and more Nigerian universities with no registration or paywall. Both tools are completely free to use.
“I handle everything from product design and engineering to deployment and research. My background as an ICT Lecturer and NLP/AI researcher meant I could move quickly from identifying the problem to shipping a working product,” Duru said.
She has certainly selected key issues to tackle. Nigeria loses an estimated NGN3.5 trillion annually to preventable crop failures, yet existing precision agriculture tools are built for high-bandwidth environments and expensive devices that most smallholder farmers simply cannot afford.
“There is no open, accessible, region-specific yield prediction tool built for the African farmer. For NaijaLearn-AI: mainstream AI tutors like ChatGPT or Khan Academy assume reliable broadband and English fluency, and none are calibrated for Nigerian university curricula or local languages. I spotted both gaps from direct experience and built the solutions myself,” said Duru.
The startup is currently self-funded and bootstrapped.
“As the sole founder and developer, I have been able to move fast and keep costs low,” Duru said.
“Both tools are newly-launched. The focus so far has been on getting the product right rather than aggressive marketing. NaijaLearn-AI is live and publicly accessible, and AgriAI is available on the Play Store. Early feedback from the developer and academic communities has been encouraging, and I am now shifting focus toward user growth.”

articles.title: How an Ericsson Castoff Became the Backbone of India’s Fibre Internet: The GX Group Story
articles.text:
How an Ericsson Castoff Became the Backbone of India’s Fibre Internet: The GX Group Story
GX Group grew from an acquired Ericsson business into a global telecom equipment manufacturer and is now investing Rs 500 crore to produce photonics chips in India.
Every time a fibre broadband connection reaches an Indian home, there's a good chance the equipment routing that signal was built by GX Group, a company most Indians have never heard of, despite its gear sitting inside networks run by Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea's You Broadband, and state-owned BSNL.
The company built from an Ericsson castoff
GX Group's origin story explains its unusual DNA. It started in 2002 as Genexis, a European broadband equipment maker; its India inflection point came in 2013, when it acquired Ericsson's end-user equipment business from Sweden and expanded pan-India on the back of it. Rebranded GX Group in 2018, it is now a strange hybrid: a Netherlands-headquartered multinational whose CEO, Paritosh Prajapati, has spent a decade turning India from a market it sells into, into the global hub it designs and manufactures from.
The product line is about as far from consumer glamour as manufacturing gets: Gigabit Passive Optical Network (GPON) gear that runs fibre broadband networks, plus Wi-Fi routers, enterprise switches, and IoT devices supplied across Asia, Europe, and Africa. Nobody buys a GPON gateway because they love the brand. They buy it because it has to work, reliably, inside infrastructure millions depend on without thinking about it.
That unglamorous positioning paid off when India's telecom production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme launched. In February 2023, GX became the first telecom gear manufacturer to meet its PLI targets and actually receive the incentives, with the Department of Telecommunications confirming its India arm was the first shortlisted entity to get a cheque, ahead of VVDN Technologies and Commscope India.
From domestic supplier to acquirer of European firms
The growth numbers tell one part of the story. In mid-2024, Prajapati said the company had posted 40% year-on-year growth in consecutive years and projected revenue rising from Rs 300 crore to Rs 500 crore by FY26, with capacity up nearly fivefold since its facility opened. He committed roughly Rs 100 crore to a new manufacturing site, invested in a Chennai R&D centre, and anticipated a 120% export jump to telcos across Africa, Europe, and Southeast Asia by shifting from exporting software to hardware.
The more telling move came in March 2025, when GX did something Indian telecom manufacturers almost never do: it acquired a European company. Ping Communication, a Swiss broadband CPE maker owned by Norway's Heimgard Group, brought a 20-year legacy, roughly $30 million in revenue, and entrenched supplier relationships with Telmex and America Movil, two of Latin America's largest operators. Prajapati called it a milestone in the "Make in India for the World" journey, targeting $50 million in LATAM revenue by 2026 in a region heading toward 134 million home broadband passes by 2027. Distribution deals followed: Ingram Micro India in June 2025, Calculus Networks for Latin America in December, alongside Oman's Al Jassar Group for the Middle East.
The Rs 500 crore photonics bet
The clearest sign of ambitions beyond assembly came in October 2025, when GX launched GX Quantum Photonics Pvt Ltd to build India's first photonics chip development, manufacturing, and R&D hub. The Rs 500 crore Phase 1 is backed by Invest International of the Netherlands and a partnership with SMART Photonics BV, a Dutch leader in indium phosphide photonic integrated circuits, the components that move light through optical networks, LiDAR, and quantum devices.
The plan is unusually concrete: a Manesar headquarters, a manufacturing facility in Bhiwadi, Rajasthan, Chennai R&D expansion, and over 300 direct jobs at a company employing around 250 people in India. Operations commence by Q1 FY27, with locally made chips reaching the market by October 2026, targeting a $50 billion opportunity spanning AI data centres, 5G/6G, EV LiDAR, and quantum communication. If that rollout lands on schedule, GX would produce photonics chips in India months before most headline semiconductor fabs produce anything at all.
Why this story matters
GX Group runs against the familiar Indian manufacturing narrative of cheap labour, thin margins, and assembly for someone else's brand. It began by buying a business Ericsson no longer wanted, used the PLI scheme better than anyone, and now reverses the usual technology flow: acquiring European firms and pushing India-made hardware into Latin America through Swiss channels. Nobody sees a GPON gateway and wonders where it came from. But behind fibre connections from Bengaluru to Mexico City, there's a reasonable chance GX built the box, and by this October, the chips inside may be Indian too.

articles.title: Cada vez hay que entrar más tarde y salir antes de los hoteles. La razón es simple: es otra excusa para cobrar más
articles.text:
Organizas tus vacaciones, reservas un hotel, y el aviso suele ser siempre el mismo: entrada a partir de las 15 horas. Para quienes llevan muchas maletas y llegan pronto eso provoca más de un quebradero de cabeza, y los hoteles lo saben bien. De hecho, están haciendo caja con ello.
Los horarios hoteleros cambian. Antes de 2020, era normal que la hora de entrada (check-in) fuese a las 14:00 y la hora de salida (check-out) fuese a las 12:00. Desde la reapertura de los hoteles tras la pandemia, las cadenas han ido empujando esos horarios hacia otros que desde luego hacen más sencilla su operativa. Hoy en día es habitual encontrarse con que el check-in no se puede hacer antes de las 15:00 y el check-out es a las 11:00 o las 12:00.
Las "kellys" tienen un punto muy válido. Hay un argumento razonable para este cambio: como explica un portavoz de Hotusa en El País, estos horarios garantizan que los equipos de limpieza tienen tiempo suficiente para dejar las habitaciones impecables. Quienes hacen esa limpieza, las llamadas kellys, lo confirman, y aclaran que esas cuatro horas les dan margen de maniobra porque la media es que cada trabajadora limpie entre 20 y 30 habitaciones al día. Eso es totalmente lógico, pero es que los hoteles también están sacando partido de la circunstancia.
Bienvenidos al "Early check-in" y al "Late check-out". Aunque ninguna cadena hotelera lo reconoce de forma explícita, una portavoz de Barceló si admitía que esto abre una nueva vía de negocio. En los últimos tiempos han aparecido las opciones "early check-in" y "late check-out" en varias cadenas hoteleras para que los clientes puedan entrar entre una y dos horas antes y salir entre una y dos horas después. Esas opciones, por supuesto, tienen un coste extra que hace que los hoteles puedan a su vez tener una vía de ingresos adicional con la que antes no contaban.
Si eres cliente fiel, puedes entrar antes y salir después. Otras cadenas ofrecen esos horarios ampliados a los miembros de sus programas de fidelización. Marriott permite a sus clientes del programa Gold Elite salir dos horas más tarde con un mínimo de 25 noches al año. Los del programa Platinum Elite tienen 50 noches anuales. Hyatt, Hotusa y Meliá hacen lo mismo. El patrón es idéntico en todos los casos: el acceso flexible a los horarios no es un derecho del huésped, sino un privilegio del cliente fidelizado.
La trampa de los servicios de fidelización. Los programas de puntos de las cadenas hoteleras funcionan sobre una premisa inquietante: si concentras todas tus estancias en una sola marca hotelera, recuperas servicios que antes eran estándar para cualquier cliente. Esos early check-in y late check-out son el ejemplo más claro, pero en la lista están otros beneficios como mejoras para la habitación, desayunos gratuitos, accesos a salas ejecutivas o servicios añadidos de conectividad. Lo que antes era cortesía ahora es una recompensa por tu lealtad. Una lealtad que, eso sí, pagas mientras pierdes cierta capacidad de elección.
Una idea fantástica salvo para el turista ocasional. Las cadenas consultadas en el texto coinciden en la misma idea: estos cambios permiten mejorar la experiencia del cliente frecuente, y a la vez hacen posible una gestión más eficiente de los recursos. Lo que no dicen es que el modelo tiene un ganador claro, y no es el viajero ocasional. El turista que viaja dos semanas al año, llega a su destino en un vuelo de madrugada y reserva a través de un operador turístico convencional está condenado. Paga una tarifa más alta, no acumula puntos canjeables y espera horas en el lobby o se ve obligado a pagar un extra.

articles.title: StrongestLayer Raises $4.1 Million in Seed Funding Extension
articles.text:
Cybersecurity startup StrongestLayer today announced raising $4.1 million in a seed funding extension round, bringing the company’s total seed investment to $9.3 million.
The fresh funding round was led by Inovia Capital, with additional support from LaunchPod, Alumni Ventures, an angel investor, and previous backer Sorenson Capital.
The company emerged from stealth mode last year.
Founded in 2024, San Francisco-based StrongestLayer provides an AI-native email security platform designed to stop modern email threats that evade traditional solutions.
According to the company, its analysis of thousands of detections between December 2025 and February 2026 has revealed that one-third of attacks cannot be detected through pattern-matching and behavioral techniques.
Using advanced reasoning and intent analysis, StrongestLayer’s platform uses context to reason, which allows it to identify attacks that it has not seen before. The startup tackles adversary-in-the-middle, advanced phishing, and business email compromise (BEC) attacks.
The system, StrongestLayer says, creates arguments for legitimacy and maliciousness, and relies on evidence analysis to reach a verdict.
StrongestLayer will use the new investment to fuel its go-to-market strategy and platform expansion efforts.
“Every generation of email security was built to recognize attacks it had seen before. That worked when attackers reused templates and infrastructure. It does not work when every attack is unique. We didn’t build a better filter. We built a system that reasons about whether a message is legitimate and whether it intends harm,” said StrongestLayer co-founder and CEO Alan LeFort.
